stem: A 32-year-old woman is admitted with acute ascending motor weakness and areflexia that began 48 hours ago. Vital capacity is declining, and lumbar puncture demonstrates albuminocytologic dissociation. The family inquires why high-dose oral or intravenous corticosteroids should not be added to her treatment regimen of intravenous immunoglobulin. What is the evidence-based rationale for avoiding corticosteroids in acute GBS?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Corticosteroids trigger sudden conversion of demyelinating neuropathy into axonal motor neuron disease

options.label: B
options.text: Corticosteroids induce irreversible autoimmune glomerulonephritis when combined with intravenous immunoglobulin

options.label: C
options.text: Corticosteroids fail to confer clinical efficacy in randomized trials and can impair peripheral nerve remyelination

options.label: D
options.text: Corticosteroids accelerate the enzymatic clearance and metabolic degradation of intravenous immunoglobulin

options.label: E
options.text: Corticosteroids directly stimulate bacterial proliferation in previously infected gastrointestinal tracts

explanation: Multiple large randomized controlled trials (including Cochrane systematic reviews) have demonstrated that corticosteroids (oral or intravenous) are ineffective in acute Guillain-Barre syndrome and may actually delay motor recovery and impede axonal remyelination. In contrast, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and therapeutic plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) are proven, equally effective first-line disease-modifying therapies for GBS.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 21-year-old woman with epilepsy well-controlled on valproate has lamotrigine added to her regimen. Two weeks later, she develops high fever, oral mucosal ulcerations, conjunctival injection, and a rapidly spreading erythematous macular rash with full-thickness epidermal sloughing (Stevens-Johnson syndrome). Why did the combination of these two agents dramatically increase her susceptibility to this life-threatening drug reaction?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation markedly prolonging half-life

options.label: B
options.text: Lamotrigine displaces valproate from albumin triggering acute hepatotoxicity

options.label: C
options.text: Both medications competitively block renal tubular clearance of metabolites

options.label: D
options.text: Valproate induces skin keratinocyte major histocompatibility class II antigens

options.label: E
options.text: Lamotrigine accelerates valproate mitochondrial beta-oxidation breakdown

explanation: Valproate is a potent inhibitor of hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (specifically UGT1A4 and UGT2B7), the primary clearance pathway for lamotrigine. Co-administration more than doubles lamotrigine's elimination half-life and dramatically increases circulating levels. If lamotrigine is not started at less than half the normal starting dose and titrated very slowly, patients face a severe risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN).
high_yield_pearl: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation, more than doubling lamotrigine levels and dramatically increasing the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

stem: A 9-year-old child is evaluated for classroom staring spells. During an observed episode, she suddenly stops speaking for seven seconds with rapid eye blinking, then immediately resumes reading her textbook at the exact sentence where she left off, completely unaware that any time elapsed. Which clinical feature definitively distinguishes this absence seizure from a focal impaired-awareness seizure of temporal lobe origin?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Instantaneous recovery to baseline cognitive function without a postictal confusional period

options.label: B
options.text: Presence of subtle bilateral facial automatisms during the period of unresponsiveness

options.label: C
options.text: Occurrence of brief retrograde amnesia encompassing events prior to the seizure

options.label: D
options.text: Complete absence of any motor movements during the entire episode duration

options.label: E
options.text: Preceding visceral epigastric rising sensation lasting thirty seconds

explanation: The critical distinguishing feature between typical absence seizures and focal impaired-awareness (complex partial) seizures is the duration and postictal state. Typical absence seizures last brief seconds (<10-15 s) and resolve instantly with immediate, seamless return to baseline activity and zero postictal confusion. In contrast, focal impaired-awareness seizures last longer (1-2 minutes), often feature complex automatisms, and characteristically leave the patient with minutes of postictal confusion.
high_yield_pearl: Absence seizures last seconds and end instantaneously without postictal confusion; focal impaired-awareness seizures last minutes and have prominent postictal confusion.

stem: A 25-year-old man who squeezed an infected furuncle in his nasolabial fold develops high fever, periorbital edema, proptosis, and an inability to abduct his right eye beyond the midline. High-resolution contrast MRI confirms septic cavernous sinus thrombosis. Why is the abducens nerve (cranial nerve VI) typically the first and most severely damaged cranial nerve in cavernous sinus thrombosis?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: It traverses freely through the central venous lumen alongside the internal carotid artery

options.label: B
options.text: It is protected within a fibrous sheath in the rigid lateral dural wall

options.label: C
options.text: It receives precarious arterial microvascular supply from the ophthalmic artery

options.label: D
options.text: It exits the skull base through the superior orbital fissure outside the annulus

options.label: E
options.text: It carries primary parasympathetic fibers exquisitely sensitive to tissue hypoxia

explanation: The cavernous sinus is a unique venous structure. Cranial nerves III, IV, V1, and V2 are embedded within the protective fibrous dural tissue of the lateral wall. In contrast, the abducens nerve (CN VI) runs freely suspended inside the central cavernous sinus venous lumen, directly adjacent to the cavernous portion of the internal carotid artery. Consequently, CN VI is the earliest and most vulnerable structure injured during cavernous sinus inflammation or thrombosis.
high_yield_pearl: The abducens nerve (CN VI) runs freely inside the central cavernous sinus lumen (not the lateral wall), making it most vulnerable to cavernous sinus thrombosis.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with generalized epilepsy managed with valproate conceives unexpectedly. High-resolution anatomical fetal ultrasound at eighteen weeks reveals a lumbar neural tube defect (myelomeningocele) and mild ventriculomegaly, with markedly elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein. What cellular biochemical mechanism underlies valproate-induced neural tube defects during early embryogenesis?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Inhibition of histone deacetylases and antagonism of folate-dependent one-carbon metabolism

options.label: B
options.text: Selective blockage of neural crest cell migration via cadherin downregulation

options.label: C
options.text: Direct mutagenesis causing trinucleotide expansion in homeobox developmental genes

options.label: D
options.text: Destruction of fetal thyroid follicles resulting in profound intrauterine cretinism

options.label: E
options.text: Arrest of embryonic cardiac looping via endocardial cushion apoptosis

explanation: Valproate is the most teratogenic antiseizure medication, conferring a 1-2% risk of neural tube defects (spina bifida aperta / myelomeningocele). Valproate interferes with folate-mediated one-carbon metabolism, downregulates folate receptors, and acts as a potent inhibitor of histone deacetylases (HDACs), inducing chromatin remodeling and aberrant gene expression during neural tube closure (days 24-28 of embryonic development).
high_yield_pearl: Valproate is a potent teratogen that causes neural tube defects by inhibiting histone deacetylases (HDACs) and antagonizing folate metabolism.

stem: A 64-year-old man suffers an ischemic stroke involving the caudal midbrain tegmentum at the level of the inferior colliculi, directly transecting the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles. Which clinical manifestation would be expected on neurological examination?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Bilateral intention tremor and severe appendicular ataxia

options.label: B
options.text: Contralateral hemiparesis and ipsilateral oculomotor palsy

options.label: C
options.text: Isolated ipsilateral Horner syndrome and hoarseness

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of pain and temperature on the contralateral body only

options.label: E
options.text: Isolated vertical gaze palsy with preserved convergence

explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncles carry dentatorubrothalamic projections from both cerebellar hemispheres. They decussate completely in the caudal midbrain tegmentum at the level of the inferior colliculus. A focal lesion directly across this decussation transects efferents from BOTH hemispheres, causing bilateral intention tremor and severe bilateral appendicular ataxia.
high_yield_pearl: A lesion transecting the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles in the caudal midbrain causes bilateral intention tremor and limb ataxia.

stem: A 45-year-old man in convulsive status epilepticus remains in persistent electrographic and clinical seizure activity at thirty-five minutes despite full weight-based intravenous lorazepam, fosphenytoin, and levetiracetam infusions. He is intubated and started on a continuous propofol infusion with continuous bedside electroencephalography. What specific electroencephalographic pattern is the primary therapeutic target when titrating general anesthetics in refractory status epilepticus?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Burst suppression pattern with periods of generalized flatline inactivity

options.label: B
options.text: Continuous generalized high-voltage polymorphic delta background slowing

options.label: C
options.text: Symmetrical frontally predominant sleep spindles and vertex K-complexes

options.label: D
options.text: Periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges occurring once every two seconds

options.label: E
options.text: Continuous low-voltage fast beta activity exceeding twenty-five hertz

explanation: Refractory status epilepticus (persisting despite benzodiazepine and second-line ASM) requires continuous intravenous anesthetic infusions (propofol, midazolam, or pentobarbital). Anesthetics are titrated to continuous electroencephalographic (cEEG) cessation of all electrographic seizure activity or to a burst-suppression pattern (brief bursts of brain electrical activity separated by 5-15 seconds of flatline isoelectric silence) maintained for 24-48 hours.
high_yield_pearl: In refractory status epilepticus, continuous IV anesthetics are titrated on EEG to achieve a burst suppression pattern or complete electrographic seizure cessation.

stem: A 35-year-old woman taking topiramate for focal epilepsy presents with acute severe right flank pain radiating to her groin and gross hematuria. Non-contrast CT confirms a calcium phosphate nephrolithiasis. Serum chemistry shows a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with a serum bicarbonate of 17 mEq/L. What enzymatic inhibition explains both her systemic acidosis and her predisposition to kidney stone formation?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition reducing renal proximal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption

options.label: B
options.text: Xanthine oxidase inhibition promoting accumulation of insoluble purine crystals

options.label: C
options.text: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition decreasing renal synthesis of protective prostaglandins

options.label: D
options.text: Succinate dehydrogenase inhibition disrupting the mitochondrial Krebs cycle

options.label: E
options.text: Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase inhibition producing severe hypocalcemia and tetany

explanation: Topiramate is a sulfamate-substituted monosaccharide that weakly inhibits carbonic anhydrase (isozymes II and IV) in renal proximal tubule cells. This causes impaired bicarbonate reabsorption, leading to alkaline urine, systemic non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, and decreased urinary citrate excretion (hypocitraturia). Low citrate combined with alkaline urine precipitates calcium phosphate kidney stones.
high_yield_pearl: Topiramate inhibits carbonic anhydrase, causing metabolic acidosis, hypocitraturia, and calcium phosphate kidney stones (nephrolithiasis).

stem: A 24-year-old man who has been taking phenytoin for two years presents with progressive, firm, fibrous overgrowth of his gums that now covers nearly half the crowns of his anterior teeth. Biopsy of the gingival tissue shows extensive collagen deposition and hyperplastic stroma without malignant atypia. Which growth factor overexpressed in response to phenytoin mediates this gingival fibrous hyperplasia?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Platelet-derived growth factor stimulating gingival fibroblast proliferation

options.label: B
options.text: Vascular endothelial growth factor inducing mucosal capillary cavernomas

options.label: C
options.text: Epidermal growth factor driving squamous epithelial keratinization

options.label: D
options.text: Insulin-like growth factor 1 causing generalized mucosal acromegaloid hypertrophy

options.label: E
options.text: Tumor necrosis factor alpha activating stromal matrix metalloproteinases

explanation: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia in up to 50% of chronic users. Phenytoin and its metabolites stimulate the expression of platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) in gingival fibroblasts, which drives excessive synthesis of collagen and proteoglycans. Good oral hygiene reduces severity, and regression typically occurs after drug discontinuation.
high_yield_pearl: Phenytoin-induced gingival hyperplasia is mediated by increased platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) stimulating fibroblast collagen synthesis.

stem: A 57-year-old man presents with acute vertigo, intractable nausea, severe dysphagia, and hoarseness. Neurological examination reveals left Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), loss of pain and temperature on the left face and right body, left cerebellar limb ataxia, and an absent left gag reflex with the uvula deviating to the right. Motor strength is 5/5 bilaterally, and dorsal column sensation is intact. What artery has occluded, and damage to which cranial nerve nucleus produces his dysphagia and hoarseness?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery; nucleus ambiguus (cranial nerves IX and X)

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery; facial motor nucleus (cranial nerve VII)

options.label: C
options.text: Anterior spinal artery; hypoglossal motor nucleus (cranial nerve XII)

options.label: D
options.text: Superior cerebellar artery; motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V)

options.label: E
options.text: Paramedian basilar branches; abducens motor nucleus (cranial nerve VI)

explanation: This is lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, caused by occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery. Key features include: nucleus ambiguus damage (CN IX and X) causing dysphagia, hoarseness, and loss of gag reflex; spinal trigeminal nucleus (ipsilateral facial pain/temp); spinothalamic tract (contralateral body pain/temp); inferior cerebellar peduncle (ipsilateral ataxia); and descending sympathetic tract (ipsilateral Horner syndrome). Motor strength is completely spared because corticospinal tracts lie ventrally in the medial medulla.
high_yield_pearl: Wallenberg syndrome (PICA occlusion) impairs the nucleus ambiguus, causing dysphagia, hoarseness, and absent gag reflex, with 'crossed' thermoanalgesia and Horner syndrome.

stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the clinic due to poor linear growth, excessive thirst, and progressive difficulty reading off the board at school. Visual field examination reveals bitemporal hemianopsia. Sagittal MRI shows a partially cystic, calcified sellar and suprasellar mass that displaces the optic chiasm upward. Aspiration yields viscous, dark brown fluid resembling 'crankcase motor oil' that contains abundant cholesterol crystals. From which embryonic precursor did this neoplasm develop?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Rathke pouch diverticulum of the oral cavity surface ectoderm

options.label: B
options.text: Diencephalic neuroectodermal outgrowth forming the neurohypophysis

options.label: C
options.text: Mesodermal paraxial condensations surrounding the primitive chorda

options.label: D
options.text: Neural crest cells migrating into the first pharyngeal arch complex

options.label: E
options.text: Endodermal epithelium derived from the ventral wall of the foregut

explanation: Craniopharyngiomas are benign suprasellar tumors derived from remnants of Rathke pouch, an ectodermal outpocketing of the primitive stomodeum (oral cavity roof) that normally forms the anterior pituitary. They typically exhibit cystic components containing rich 'motor oil' fluid filled with glistening cholesterol crystals, peripheral rim calcifications on CT, and compression of the optic chiasm (bitemporal hemianopsia) and pituitary stalk.
high_yield_pearl: Craniopharyngiomas derive from Rathke pouch (surface ectoderm), contain 'motor oil' fluid with cholesterol crystals, calcify, and cause bitemporal hemianopsia.

stem: A 5-day-old neonate born at 39 weeks develops fever, lethargy, poor feeding, and a bulging fontanelle. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis confirms acute bacterial meningitis. The physician orders ampicillin and cefotaxime rather than ceftriaxone. What dangerous neonatal pharmacological adverse effect specifically mandates the avoidance of ceftriaxone in this age group?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Displacement of bilirubin from albumin leading to kernicterus brainstem injury

options.label: B
options.text: Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus causing acute pulmonary hypertension

options.label: C
options.text: Irreversible inhibition of renal tubular growth leading to nephrocalcinosis

options.label: D
options.text: Severe chondrotoxicity producing permanent epiphyseal growth plate arrest

options.label: E
options.text: Complete bone marrow aplasia via mitochondrial ribosome subunit blockade

explanation: Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates (<28 days old) because it strongly binds to albumin and displaces unconjugated bilirubin, markedly increasing free bilirubin levels and the risk of bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus). Additionally, ceftriaxone precipitates with intravenous calcium-containing solutions (e.g., parenteral nutrition) in neonatal lungs and kidneys. Cefotaxime has low protein binding and does not cause biliary sludging or kernicterus.
high_yield_pearl: Ceftriaxone is contraindicated in neonates because it displaces bilirubin from albumin, causing kernicterus, and can precipitate with calcium.

stem: A 6-month-old infant with tuberous sclerosis develops clusters of myoclonic flexor spasms (salaam spasms) on awakening, with an EEG demonstrating hypsarrhythmia (West syndrome). The pediatric neurologist prescribes vigabatrin. What irreversible, dose-cumulative sensory toxicity mandates serial baseline and ongoing ophthalmologic visual field evaluations in this infant?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Permanent bilateral concentric visual field constriction from retinal toxicity

options.label: B
options.text: Accelerated posterior subcapsular cataract formation in bilateral lenses

options.label: C
options.text: Rapid fibrovascular proliferation leading to tractional retinal detachment

options.label: D
options.text: Ischemic optic neuropathy resulting from choroidal microvascular occlusion

options.label: E
options.text: Acute closed-angle glaucoma secondary to anterior pupillary block

explanation: Vigabatrin is an irreversible inhibitor of GABA transaminase (the enzyme that degrades GABA), increasing brain GABA concentrations; it is the drug of choice for infantile spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis. However, vigabatrin carries a black-box warning for permanent, irreversible concentric peripheral visual field constriction in 30-40% of patients due to retinal amacrine and ganglion cell toxicity.
high_yield_pearl: Vigabatrin (GABA transaminase inhibitor) is first-line for infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis but can cause irreversible peripheral visual field constriction.

stem: A 61-year-old hypertensive man develops acute right-sided dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia without motor weakness or sensory loss. Diffusion-weighted MRI reveals an acute ischemic infarction isolated to the right middle cerebellar peduncle (brachium pontis). Which afferent fiber tract has been directly transected by this lesion?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Transverse pontocerebellar fibers from contralateral pontine nuclei

options.label: B
options.text: Dorsal spinocerebellar fibers ascending from Clarke column

options.label: C
options.text: Dentatothalamic projection fibers directed to the ventral thalamus

options.label: D
options.text: Primary vestibular fibers emerging from scarpa ganglion

options.label: E
options.text: Rubrospinal motor projections descending to the cervical spinal cord

explanation: The middle cerebellar peduncle (brachium pontis) is the largest cerebellar peduncle and contains exclusively afferent fibers: the transverse pontocerebellar tract. Corticopontine fibers from the contralateral cerebral cortex synapse in the basal pontine nuclei, whose axons cross the midline and travel via the MCP to enter the cerebellar hemisphere.
high_yield_pearl: The middle cerebellar peduncle consists exclusively of afferent transverse pontocerebellar fibers arising from the contralateral pontine nuclei.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents with progressive weakness in both legs, distal muscle wasting, and pes cavus. Electrodiagnostic testing reveals motor nerve conduction velocities of 52 m/s (normal >50 m/s), but compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes are severely reduced to 1.2 mV (normal >5.0 mV). Which fundamental histopathologic feature distinguishes this axonal hereditary neuropathy (CMT2) from the demyelinating form (CMT1)?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Concentric hypertrophy of Schwann cells forming prominent onion bulbs surrounding myelinated axons

options.label: B
options.text: Wallerian-like degeneration and loss of large myelinated axons without prominent Schwann cell hyperplasia

options.label: C
options.text: Segmental breakdown of myelin sheaths with marked sparing of underlying neurofilament integrity

options.label: D
options.text: Perivascular CD8-positive lymphocytic infiltration into the endoneurium with microglial nodules

options.label: E
options.text: Extracellular deposition of transthyretin amyloid fibrils within the epineurial connective tissue

explanation: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is divided into demyelinating (CMT1) and axonal (CMT2) forms. CMT1 is characterized by severe slowing of conduction velocities (<38 m/s) and 'onion-bulb' Schwann cell hyperplasia secondary to repeated demyelination and remyelination. In contrast, CMT2 is a primary axonal neuropathy characterized by preserved or mildly reduced conduction velocities (>38-50 m/s), markedly reduced CMAP/SNAP amplitudes, and biopsy evidence of Wallerian-like axonal loss without Schwann cell proliferation.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 19-year-old college freshman with culture-confirmed Neisseria meningitidis bacteremia abruptly deteriorates over three hours, developing widespread purpura fulminans, refractory shock, profound metabolic acidosis, and bilateral flank pain. Autopsy reveals extensive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage with cortical necrosis (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome). What physiological failure directly caused his circulatory collapse?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Acute primary adrenal insufficiency with severe cortisol and aldosterone depletion

options.label: B
options.text: Massive release of myocardial depressant factors from pulmonary alveoli

options.label: C
options.text: Rupture of internal carotid mycotic aneurysms into the subarachnoid space

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of medullary sympathetic outflow from cerebellar tonsillar herniation

options.label: E
options.text: Complete heart block from septic embolization into the cardiac bundle of His

explanation: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is a devastating complication of severe meningococcemia characterized by endotoxin-driven disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), purpuric rash, and bilateral adrenal gland hemorrhage. Adrenal destruction results in acute primary adrenal insufficiency with profound loss of cortisol and aldosterone, causing vasopressor-refractory hypovolemic and distributive shock.
high_yield_pearl: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome in meningococcemia causes bilateral adrenal cortical hemorrhage, acute adrenal crisis, and refractory shock.

stem: A 32-year-old man with focal epilepsy takes 300 mg daily of phenytoin with a steady-state serum concentration of 9 mcg/mL (therapeutic range 10-20 mcg/mL). Due to persistent seizures, his dosage is increased by 33% to 400 mg daily. Two weeks later, he presents with severe ataxia, coarse horizontal nystagmus, and confusion, with a serum level of 36 mcg/mL. What pharmacokinetic principle explains this disproportionate level increase?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Transition from first-order to zero-order saturation elimination kinetics

options.label: B
options.text: Marked down-regulation of renal tubular organic anion secretory pumps

options.label: C
options.text: Auto-inhibition of gastrointestinal enterocyte P-glycoprotein transport

options.label: D
options.text: Progressive displacement from serum albumin by endogenous fatty acids

options.label: E
options.text: Allosteric conformational activation of hepatic cytochrome P450 oxidases

explanation: Phenytoin displays Michaelis-Menten non-linear pharmacokinetics. At low concentrations, elimination is first-order (rate proportional to concentration). Near therapeutic levels (10-20 mcg/mL), hepatic microsomal clearance enzymes (CYP2C9 and CYP2C19) become fully saturated, shifting elimination to zero-order kinetics (fixed amount cleared per unit time). Small incremental dosage increases then cause massive, toxic jumps in serum concentration.
high_yield_pearl: Phenytoin follows zero-order (saturation) kinetics near therapeutic range, meaning small dose increases can trigger massive jumps in serum level and toxicity.

stem: A 17-year-old high school student presents after suffering a first generalized tonic-clonic seizure following overnight studying. On direct questioning, he admits that for the past year he has had brief, shock-like morning jerks in both arms that occasionally cause him to drop breakfast items or his toothbrush. EEG shows generalized 4- to 6-Hz polyspike-and-wave discharges. Which antiseizure medication represents the drug of choice for this condition, and which class must be avoided due to the risk of paradoxically aggravating these myoclonic seizures?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Valproate is first-line; sodium-channel blockers like carbamazepine must be avoided

options.label: B
options.text: Carbamazepine is first-line; broad-spectrum agents like valproate must be avoided

options.label: C
options.text: Ethosuximide is first-line; benzodiazepines like clonazepam must be avoided

options.label: D
options.text: Phenytoin is first-line; calcium-channel modulators like gabapentin must be avoided

options.label: E
options.text: Phenobarbital is first-line; synaptic vesicle ligands like levetiracetam must be avoided

explanation: Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME, Janz syndrome) presents in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks (often dropping objects after waking), generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and occasional absence seizures, with 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave EEG. The drug of choice is broad-spectrum valproate (or levetiracetam/lamotrigine in women of childbearing potential). Narrow-spectrum sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin) and GABA analogs (gabapentin, vigabatrin) can paradoxically worsen myoclonic seizures.
high_yield_pearl: JME (morning arm jerks + GTC) is treated with valproate; narrow-spectrum sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin) can worsen myoclonic seizures.

stem: A newborn infant is found to have a harsh holosystolic murmur and multiple well-circumscribed echogenic masses within the ventricular myocardium on echocardiography, consistent with cardiac rhabdomyomas. Wood's lamp examination discloses several hypomelanotic macules across the torso. What is the typical clinical course of these cardiac masses, and what life-threatening renal complication is this child at risk for developing in young adulthood?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Spontaneous rhabdomyoma regression; severe retroperitoneal bleed from angiomyolipoma

options.label: B
options.text: Rapid malignant sarcomatous degeneration; bilateral clear cell renal carcinomas

options.label: C
options.text: Progression to fatal dilated cardiomyopathy; diffuse renal medullary amyloidosis

options.label: D
options.text: Metastasis to regional thoracic nodes; end-stage renal medullary cystic disease

options.label: E
options.text: Calcific aortic stenosis by age five; recurrent staghorn calculus formation

explanation: Cardiac rhabdomyomas are benign hamartomas strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis (>50% have TSC). Remarkably, most cardiac rhabdomyomas spontaneously regress during childhood as cardiomyocytes mature. However, TSC patients are at high lifetime risk for bilateral renal angiomyolipomas (composed of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and adipose tissue), which are prone to aneurysmal rupture and massive retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
high_yield_pearl: Cardiac rhabdomyomas in tuberous sclerosis typically undergo spontaneous regression; renal angiomyolipomas can cause catastrophic retroperitoneal bleeding.

stem: A 39-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis who has been receiving natalizumab for three years develops progressive apathy, cognitive slowing, right homonymous hemianopia, and gait ataxia. Brain MRI demonstrates asymmetric, non-enhancing, scalloped white matter hyperintensities involving subcortical U-fibers without mass effect. Cerebrospinal fluid PCR confirms JC virus reactivation. Which specific glial cell type undergoes lytic infection and destruction by this polyomavirus?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Myelinating oligodendrocytes exhibiting enlarged glassy basophilic nuclei

options.label: B
options.text: Protoplasmic astrocytes forming extensive fibrillary glial scars

options.label: C
options.text: Resident parenchymal microglia acting as central antigen-presenting cells

options.label: D
options.text: Ciliated ependymal cells lining the walls of the cerebral aqueduct

options.label: E
options.text: Endothelial cells forming the continuous tight junctions of brain capillaries

explanation: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML) is caused by reactivation of the JC polyomavirus in immunocompromised individuals or those on immunosuppressive monoclonals (e.g., natalizumab, efalizumab). JC virus selectively infects and lyses oligodendrocytes, leading to widespread multifocal demyelination. On histology, oligodendrocytes show enlarged nuclei packed with glassy basophilic viral inclusion bodies.
high_yield_pearl: PML results from JC virus reactivation in immunosuppressed patients (or on natalizumab), selectively destroying oligodendrocytes to cause multifocal demyelination.

stem: A 49-year-old man hospitalized with acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (GBS) requires mechanical ventilation. On hospital day 4, telemetry captures episodes of sinus bradycardia down to 32 bpm alternating with sinus tachycardia of 145 bpm. Blood pressure fluctuates between 75/40 mmHg and 215/115 mmHg without administration of vasoactive agents. What is the fundamental pathological cause of these hemodynamic fluctuations?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Ischemic necrosis of the solitary tract nucleus caused by vertebrobasilar occlusion

options.label: B
options.text: Demyelination of afferent baroreceptor nerves and efferent autonomic sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers

options.label: C
options.text: Acute catecholamine surge secondary to underlying undiagnosed adrenal pheochromocytoma

options.label: D
options.text: Autoantibody-mediated cross-reactivity directly destroying sinoatrial nodal pacemaker cells

options.label: E
options.text: Severe hypovolemia resulting from syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

explanation: Dysautonomia occurs in approximately two-thirds of patients with Guillain-Barre syndrome and is a major cause of sudden mortality. The mechanism is demyelination of both afferent baroreceptor pathways (carotid sinus and aortic arch fibers via CN IX and X) and efferent postganglionic sympathetic and parasympathetic autonomic fibers. This results in loss of central baroreflex buffering, producing dramatic swings in blood pressure, labile heart rate, sinus arrest, and tachyarrhythmias.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 46-year-old woman is diagnosed with acute pneumococcal meningitis confirmed by cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain showing Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci. The emergency physician administers intravenous dexamethasone fifteen minutes prior to the first dose of bactericidal antibiotics. What clinical outcome is specifically targeted by this timed administration of glucocorticoid therapy?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Reduction in sensorineural hearing loss and neurological disability from cytokine release

options.label: B
options.text: Direct inhibition of bacterial autolysin enzymes responsible for cell wall turnover

options.label: C
options.text: Enhancement of vancomycin penetration through the intact blood-brain barrier

options.label: D
options.text: Prevention of secondary systemic vasodilation and early septic cardiovascular collapse

options.label: E
options.text: Acceleration of cerebrospinal fluid reabsorption across the arachnoid villi

explanation: Antibiotic-induced lysis of Streptococcus pneumoniae releases cell-wall fragments (peptidoglycan and teichoic acid) that stimulate intense subarachnoid cytokine production (TNF-alpha, IL-1), worsening cerebral edema, intracranial pressure, and cochlear damage. Administering dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose blunts this hyperinflammatory cascade, significantly decreasing sensorineural hearing loss and mortality.
high_yield_pearl: Dexamethasone administered before or with the first antibiotic dose in pneumococcal meningitis reduces inflammatory hearing loss and mortality.

stem: A 54-year-old man with focal epilepsy on adjunctive lacosamide undergoes a routine electrocardiogram that demonstrates a PR interval prolongation of 240 milliseconds without QRS widening. What unique electrophysiological mechanism of action distinguishes lacosamide from traditional sodium channel blockers such as phenytoin and carbamazepine?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Selective enhancement of the slow inactivation state of voltage-gated sodium channels

options.label: B
options.text: Competitive blockade of fast inactivation gates on voltage-gated sodium channels

options.label: C
options.text: Permanent irreversible alkylation of pore-forming alpha subunits in Purkinje cells

options.label: D
options.text: Selective opening of inward rectifying potassium channels in cardiac myocytes

options.label: E
options.text: Direct inhibition of sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase in the sinoatrial node

explanation: Traditional sodium channel blockers (phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine) bind to and stabilize the fast-inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels. In contrast, lacosamide selectively enhances slow inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels, terminating sustained repetitive burst firing without affecting physiological rapid action potentials. Lacosamide can prolong the PR interval, necessitating caution in patients with cardiac conduction disease.
high_yield_pearl: Lacosamide selectively enhances the slow inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels and can cause PR interval prolongation.

stem: A 73-year-old man undergoes emergency repair of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm complicated by massive hemorrhage and profound intraoperative hypotension (mean arterial pressure below 45 mmHg for fifty minutes). Upon emergence from anesthesia, he has severe bilateral proximal shoulder and hip weakness (1/5 strength) with preserved distal hand grip (5/5) and foot dorsiflexion (5/5), resembling a 'man-in-a-barrel.' What hemodynamic and neurovascular mechanism produced this presentation?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Bilateral cortical watershed ischemia between the anterior and middle cerebral arteries

options.label: B
options.text: Embolic occlusion of the basilar artery summit causing top-of-the-basilar syndrome

options.label: C
options.text: Thrombosis of the anterior spinal artery at the level of the conus medullaris

options.label: D
options.text: Acute watershed infarction between the superior and inferior cerebellar territories

options.label: E
options.text: Bilateral internal carotid artery dissections with total hemispheric infarctions

explanation: Watershed (border zone) infarcts occur at the most distal junctions between major arterial vascular territories during severe systemic hypoperfusion (e.g., cardiac arrest, hemorrhagic shock). The anterior cortical border zone lies between the ACA and MCA territories over the high convexity motor cortex, which somatotopically controls the proximal upper and lower extremities (trunk, shoulders, thighs). Bilateral ischemia here causes 'man-in-a-barrel' syndrome: severe proximal bibrachial weakness with preserved distal hand function.
high_yield_pearl: 'Man-in-a-barrel' syndrome is caused by bilateral watershed infarction between ACA and MCA territories during profound systemic hypotension.

stem: A 53-year-old man presents with acute-onset diplopia and marked unsteadiness on his feet. Neurological examination reveals bilateral symmetric external ophthalmoplegia, bilateral ptosis, severe gait and limb ataxia, and generalized absence of deep tendon reflexes. Muscle strength is 5/5 in all four extremities, and sensory examination is normal. Serum testing is most likely to identify high-titer autoantibodies against which antigen?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Presynaptic voltage-gated potassium channels expressed on central interneurons

options.label: B
options.text: GM1 gangliosides expressed on the motor axons of the lumbosacral plexus

options.label: C
options.text: GQ1b gangliosides densely expressed on ocular motor cranial nerves and sensory spindles

options.label: D
options.text: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein localized to central oligodendroglial membranes

options.label: E
options.text: Aquaporin-4 water channels enriched on astrocytic foot processes surrounding capillaries

explanation: The clinical triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia with preserved motor strength defines Miller Fisher syndrome, a localized variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome. It is caused by molecular mimicry leading to high-titer IgG autoantibodies against GQ1b ganglioside. GQ1b is enriched in the paranodal regions of cranial nerves III, IV, and VI, as well as the large-diameter group Ia primary afferent fibers supplying muscle spindles, explaining the ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 34-year-old woman with highly active relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis is evaluated for disease-modifying therapy. Before prescribing natalizumab, her neurologist orders serum anti-JC virus antibody testing. What is the molecular mechanism of natalizumab that creates an elevated risk for progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Depletion of surface CD20 on pre-B cells preventing immunoglobulin G synthesis

options.label: B
options.text: Internalization of sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors trapping T-cells in lymph nodes

options.label: C
options.text: Blockade of alpha-4 beta-1 integrin preventing leukocyte transmigration across the blood-brain barrier

options.label: D
options.text: Inhibition of dihydroorotate dehydrogenase arresting pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis

options.label: E
options.text: Selective antagonism of complement factor C5 preventing membrane attack complex formation

explanation: Natalizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody directed against the alpha-4 subunit of alpha-4-beta-1 (VLA-4) integrin on leukocytes. By blocking VLA-4 interaction with VCAM-1 on vascular endothelial cells, it prevents leukocytes from crossing the blood-brain barrier. While highly effective in MS, this prevents normal central nervous system immune surveillance, allowing latent JC polyomavirus in oligodendrocytes to reactivate and produce opportunistic progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML).
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 71-year-old man had a blistering dermatomal rash across his right T5 dermatome six months ago that resolved completely. However, he continues to suffer from excruciating burning, electric sensations in that area, where even the light touch of a shirt produces intense pain (mechanical allodynia). What underlying neurobiological alteration in sensory pathways sustains this chronic postherpetic neuralgia?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Central dorsal horn hyperexcitability and loss of GABAergic inhibitory interneurons

options.label: B
options.text: Persistent lytic replication of active varicella virions inside Schwann cells

options.label: C
options.text: Progressive demyelination of ascending spinothalamic tracts in cervical cord

options.label: D
options.text: Autoimmune antibody blockade of postsynaptic alpha-motor endplate receptors

options.label: E
options.text: Hypertrophy of cutaneous Pacinian corpuscles within the superficial dermis

explanation: Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) is neuropathic pain persisting >3 months after herpes zoster resolution. VZV ganglionic necrosis causes both peripheral nerve damage and spinal dorsal horn reorganization: damaged sensory fibers exhibit spontaneous ectopic discharges, and death of GABAergic inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa produces central sensitization and allodynia.
high_yield_pearl: Postherpetic neuralgia is maintained by central sensitization and loss of inhibitory dorsal horn interneurons following VZV-induced ganglionitis.

stem: A 41-year-old HIV-infected man with a CD4 count of 38/uL presents with a progressive, throbbing headache, low-grade fever, and photophobia over two weeks. Lumbar puncture demonstrates an elevated opening pressure of 340 mm H2O. CSF India ink preparation shows narrow-based budding encapsulated yeasts, and cryptococcal latex agglutination is strongly positive. In addition to serial lumbar punctures to control elevated intracranial pressure, which antimicrobial induction regimen is indicated?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Liposomal amphotericin B combined with oral flucytosine for two weeks

options.label: B
options.text: High-dose oral fluconazole monotherapy administered for ten weeks

options.label: C
options.text: Intravenous voriconazole combined with caspofungin echinocandin therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole with adjunctive corticosteroids

options.label: E
options.text: Oral itraconazole maintenance therapy coupled with immediate antiretrovirals

explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis (Cryptococcus neoformans) is an opportunistic fungal infection in advanced AIDS (CD4 < 100/uL). The standard induction regimen is liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine for at least 2 weeks, followed by fluconazole consolidation. Managing elevated intracranial pressure (opening pressure >200-250 mm H2O) with therapeutic serial lumbar punctures is critical to prevent visual loss and herniation.
high_yield_pearl: Cryptococcal meningitis in AIDS requires induction with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, along with serial lumbar punctures to relieve elevated intracranial pressure.

stem: A neuroscientist records baseline high-frequency simple spikes from cerebellar Purkinje cells during repetitive limb movements. Targeted application of a glutamate receptor antagonist to parallel fibers completely abolishes these simple spikes while sparing climbing fiber input. From which interneurons do these parallel fibers originate?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Granule cells located within the cerebellar internal granular layer

options.label: B
options.text: Golgi interneurons providing feedback to mossy fiber glomeruli

options.label: C
options.text: Basket cells providing feedforward axosomatic inhibition

options.label: D
options.text: Stellate interneurons distributing axodendritic inhibition

options.label: E
options.text: Unipolar brush cells amplifying vestibular mossy fiber signals

explanation: Mossy fibers terminate on granule cells within cerebellar glomeruli. Granule cell axons ascend to the molecular layer, bifurcate into T-shaped parallel fibers, and synapse on dendrites of hundreds of Purkinje cells, driving high-frequency simple spikes. Golgi cells inhibit granule cells, while basket and stellate cells inhibit Purkinje cells.
high_yield_pearl: Mossy fibers excite granule cells whose parallel fibers ascend and bifurcate to excite Purkinje cells, generating high-frequency simple spikes.

stem: A 47-year-old man with a low-grade oligodendroglioma develops stereotyped episodes beginning with rhythmic clonic jerking of his right thumb that progressively marches over sixty seconds to involve his right fingers, wrist, forearm, arm, and right lower face without impairment of awareness. Where does this seizure activity originate and what neuroanatomical principle dictates its order of progression?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Precentral gyrus propagating sequentially along the somatic motor homunculus

options.label: B
options.text: Postcentral gyrus spreading via intracortical associative thalamic fibers

options.label: C
options.text: Supplementary motor area discharging across the anterior corpus callosum

options.label: D
options.text: Dentate cerebellar nucleus propagating through the superior peduncle

options.label: E
options.text: Subthalamic nucleus sending disinhibited signals to the globus pallidus

explanation: This patient exhibits a classic Jacksonian march, a form of focal aware motor seizure originating in the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus, Brodmann area 4). Epileptiform discharges travel contiguously across neighboring neuronal populations along the motor homunculus, sequentially recruiting adjacent anatomical representations (thumb to fingers to wrist to arm to face).
high_yield_pearl: Jacksonian march is a focal aware seizure originating in the precentral gyrus that spreads contiguously along the cortical motor homunculus.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis is evaluated for upper extremity incoordination. The examiner asks her to flex her right elbow against manual resistance, then suddenly releases his grip. Her right forearm recoils forcefully and strikes her anterior chest before arresting. What physiologic defect accounts for this examination finding?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Delayed activation of antagonist triceps braking contractions

options.label: B
options.text: Hyperactive monosynaptic stretch reflexes in the bicep tendon

options.label: C
options.text: Denervation hypersensitivity within neuromuscular endplates

options.label: D
options.text: Loss of recurrent Renshaw cell inhibition in anterior horns

options.label: E
options.text: Impaired gamma motor neuron efferent tone to muscle spindles

explanation: This demonstrates Holmes rebound phenomenon, a hallmark of ipsilateral cerebellar hemisphere disease. Normally, the cerebellum rapidly computes the sudden drop in load and immediately activates antagonist muscles (triceps) while shutting off agonists (biceps) to brake the limb. Cerebellar dysfunction delays this antagonist braking loop, causing overshoot.
high_yield_pearl: The Holmes rebound phenomenon is caused by delayed activation of antagonist muscle braking due to ipsilateral cerebellar intermediate or hemispheric pathology.

stem: A 2-year-old child presents with intractable focal seizures. Examination reveals a unilateral facial port-wine stain (nevus flammeus) strictly demarcating the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Non-contrast head CT demonstrates prominent ipsilateral parieto-occipital cortical 'tram-track' gyriform calcifications and underlying cerebral atrophy. What genetic mechanism explains the spontaneous, non-familial occurrence of this disorder?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Postzygotic somatic mosaic gain-of-function mutation in the GNAQ gene

options.label: B
options.text: Maternal uniparental disomy involving chromosome 15 imprinted alleles

options.label: C
options.text: Germline trinucleotide repeat expansion showing maternal anticipation

options.label: D
options.text: Autosomal dominant deletion of the proximal p-arm of chromosome 3

options.label: E
options.text: Mitochondrial DNA point mutation exhibiting variable tissue heteroplasmy

explanation: Sturge-Weber syndrome (encephalotrigeminal angiomatosis) is not inherited; it is caused by an activating postzygotic somatic mosaic mutation in the GNAQ gene (encoding G-alpha-q). Because the mutation occurs postzygotically in embryonic progenitor cells, it affects only a mosaic subset of cells forming capillary venules in the V1 trigeminal distribution, ipsilateral leptomeninges (leptomeningeal angioma leading to hypoperfusion, seizures, and 'tram-track' cortical calcification), and anterior eye (glaucoma).
high_yield_pearl: Sturge-Weber syndrome is caused by a somatic mosaic GNAQ mutation, causing a V1 port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angiomas, seizures, and tram-track calcifications.

stem: A 32-year-old woman in her 34th week of gestation develops new-onset focal motor seizures involving her left hand. Brain MRI demonstrates an extra-axial, dural-based, intensely enhancing mass along the right parasagittal frontoparietal convexity with a distinct dural tail sign. Biopsy demonstrates whorled syncytial clusters of spindle cells containing psammoma bodies. What hormonal characteristic of this tumor explains its accelerated clinical presentation during the third trimester?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: High expression of functional nuclear progesterone receptors driving cell growth

options.label: B
options.text: Constitutive overexpression of human chorionic gonadotropin-stimulated receptors

options.label: C
options.text: Suppression of epidermal growth factor receptor signaling by placental lactogen

options.label: D
options.text: Selective reliance on elevated circulating prolactin for angiogenic signaling

options.label: E
options.text: Inactivation of mineralocorticoid receptors by elevated free plasma aldosterone

explanation: Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells and frequently express progesterone receptors (up to 70-80% of cases). During pregnancy (particularly the third trimester when circulating progesterone levels are highest), meningiomas can rapidly enlarge and produce new-onset neurological deficits or seizures, followed by potential postpartum regression.
high_yield_pearl: Meningiomas are extra-axial dural-based tumors that express progesterone receptors, causing rapid growth and symptom onset during pregnancy.

stem: A 9-year-old boy with a history of infantile spasms and cognitive impairment presents with severe refractory morning vomiting and lethargy. Physical examination demonstrates multiple hypomelanotic ash-leaf macules and facial angiofibromas. Neuroimaging reveals an avidly enhancing 2.5-cm intraventricular mass at the foramen of Monro causing acute bilateral lateral ventriculomegaly. Targeted medical therapy that directly inhibits which enzymatic complex has proven efficacy in shrinking this specific tumor?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 mTORC1 serine/threonine kinase

options.label: B
options.text: Epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase intracellular domain

options.label: C
options.text: Anaplastic lymphoma kinase ALK catalytic fusion oncoprotein

options.label: D
options.text: Cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 regulating the G1-S checkpoint

options.label: E
options.text: Poly ADP-ribose polymerase 1 mediating single-strand DNA base repair

explanation: This patient with tuberous sclerosis has developed a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA) at the foramen of Monro, causing non-communicating hydrocephalus. Tuberous sclerosis results from mutations in TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin), which normally form a complex that inhibits Rheb GTPase. Loss of this complex leads to constitutive Rheb-mediated activation of mTORC1. The mTOR inhibitors everolimus and sirolimus directly inhibit mTORC1, reducing SEGA volume and preventing hydrocephalus.
high_yield_pearl: Tuberous sclerosis causes mTOR hyperactivation; SEGA at the foramen of Monro can be treated medically with mTOR inhibitors (everolimus/sirolimus).

stem: An 8-year-old boy bitten on the hand by a bat in an unexplored cave six weeks earlier develops fever, severe agitation, autonomic instability, and violent pharyngeal muscle spasms triggered by attempts to swallow water (hydrophobia). What motor transport protein mediated the retrograde axonal transit of this bullet-shaped virus to the spinal cord, and what pathognomonic histology is seen at autopsy?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Dynein motor proteins; eosinophilic intracytoplasmic Negri inclusion bodies

options.label: B
options.text: Kinesin motor proteins; basophilic intranuclear Cowdry A inclusion bodies

options.label: C
options.text: Myosin V molecular motors; widespread microglial nodules with neuronophagia

options.label: D
options.text: Actin filament treadmilling; diffuse amyloid plaque deposition in cortex

options.label: E
options.text: Tubulin dimer elongation; perivascular lymphocytic cuffing without inclusions

explanation: Rabies virus (bullet-shaped Rhabdovirus) binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction and travels by retrograde axoplasmic transport mediated by dynein motor proteins to the central nervous system. Histopathologically, it is characterized by pathognomonic eosinophilic intracytoplasmic Negri bodies in hippocampal pyramidal neurons and cerebellar Purkinje cells.
high_yield_pearl: Rabies travels via retrograde dynein transport to the CNS, producing hydrophobia, agitation, and pathognomonic intracytoplasmic Negri bodies in Purkinje and hippocampal cells.

stem: A 39-year-old woman with advanced spinocerebellar ataxia produces speech that is slow, slurred, and fragmented into unnatural pauses between syllables, with explosive variations in vocal volume and pitch (scanning speech). Which functional anatomical zone of the cerebellum is primarily responsible for coordinating the rhythm and articulation of speech?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Superior cerebellar vermis and adjacent intermediate paravermis

options.label: B
options.text: Bilateral flocculonodular lobes coordinating oculomotor vergence

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral neocerebellar cortex of the posterior inferior lobules

options.label: D
options.text: Fastigial projection pathways to the lateral vestibular nuclei

options.label: E
options.text: Dentatothalamic decussation within the caudal red nucleus capsule

explanation: Cerebellar dysarthria (scanning speech or ataxic dysarthria) is characterized by slow, disjointed, syllabic articulation with irregular stress and loudness. It results from damage to the superior cerebellar vermis and adjacent intermediate zone (paravermis), particularly in the left or bilateral hemispheres, which coordinate orofacial and respiratory muscles during speech articulation.
high_yield_pearl: Scanning speech (ataxic dysarthria) results from lesions involving the superior cerebellar vermis and adjacent intermediate cortex.

stem: A 68-year-old retired farmer living in the Midwest presents in August with high fever, mental confusion, prominent postural tremor, and sudden asymmetric flaccid paralysis of his right lower extremity. Deep tendon reflexes in the right patellar and Achilles tendons are completely absent without sensory deficits. CSF analysis reveals lymphocytic pleocytosis and West Nile virus IgM antibodies. What neuropathological lesion is responsible for this acute asymmetric flaccid weakness?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Direct cytolytic viral destruction of spinal cord anterior horn alpha motor neurons

options.label: B
options.text: Autoimmune demyelination of the lateral corticospinal tract in cervical cord

options.label: C
options.text: Immune complex deposition within the anterior spinal artery vascular lumen

options.label: D
options.text: Autoantibody blockade of voltage-gated calcium channels at motor terminals

options.label: E
options.text: Bilateral demyelination of peripheral motor nerve roots at the cauda equina

explanation: West Nile virus (a mosquito-borne Flavivirus) can cause a poliomyelitis-like acute flaccid paralysis syndrome. The virus has a specific tropism for spinal anterior horn alpha motor neurons, causing direct cytolytic necrosis. This manifests as acute, asymmetric, flaccid weakness with hyporeflexia/areflexia and fasciculations without sensory loss (pure lower motor neuron pattern).
high_yield_pearl: West Nile virus can cause acute asymmetric flaccid paralysis by directly destroying anterior horn motor neurons (poliomyelitis-like syndrome).

stem: A 48-year-old woman recovering from a cerebellar stroke is evaluated in the clinic. When the examiner taps her patellar tendon, her leg extends and then continues swinging back and forth like a pendulum for six oscillations before coming to rest. What neuromuscular physiological abnormality produces this pendular reflex?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of cerebellar tonic facilitatory drive to muscle stretch receptors

options.label: B
options.text: Hyperactivity of upper motor neuron corticospinal tract efferents

options.label: C
options.text: Loss of primary afferent depolarization within spinal interneurons

options.label: D
options.text: Persistent tetanic recruitment of slow-twitch motor units

options.label: E
options.text: Selective destruction of Renshaw inhibitory spinal interneurons

explanation: Pendular reflexes are a classic sign of cerebellar hypotonia. The cerebellum normally maintains baseline gamma motor neuron efferent tone and coordinates antagonist damping. With cerebellar lesions, reduced muscle tone and lack of antagonist muscle damping allow the limb to swing passively back and forth under the influence of gravity alone.
high_yield_pearl: Pendular reflexes result from cerebellar hypotonia and loss of antagonist muscle damping, allowing the limb to swing passively like a pendulum.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with high fever, severe headache, confusion, and marked nuchal rigidity. Lumbar puncture demonstrates an opening pressure of 260 mm H2O, WBC count of 2,400/uL with 92% neutrophils, protein of 280 mg/dL, and glucose of 18 mg/dL. In addition to intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone, ampicillin is added to his empiric regimen. What specific microbiological coverage justifies the addition of ampicillin in this age cohort?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Listeria monocytogenes exhibiting inherent resistance to third-generation cephalosporins

options.label: B
options.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa requiring double coverage with extended-spectrum penicillins

options.label: C
options.text: Beta-lactamase producing strains of Neisseria meningitidis endemic to adults

options.label: D
options.text: Atypical Mycoplasma hominis invading the blood-brain barrier via tight junctions

options.label: E
options.text: Methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus seeding from paranasal sinuses

explanation: Adults older than 50 years and immunocompromised patients are at increased risk for meningitis caused by Listeria monocytogenes, a facultative intracellular Gram-positive bacillus acquired through unpasteurized dairy or processed meats. Listeria is inherently resistant to all cephalosporins due to low-affinity penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), mandating the addition of ampicillin to empiric vancomycin and ceftriaxone.
high_yield_pearl: Empiric meningitis therapy in adults >50 or immunocompromised requires ampicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes, which is inherently resistant to cephalosporins.

stem: A 22-year-old collegiate runner develops progressive sensory ataxia, bilateral extensor plantar responses, marked loss of vibration and joint position sense, absent ankle and knee reflexes, and bilateral high-arched feet. Serum cobalamin and methylmalonic acid levels are normal, and rapid plasma reagin (RPR) is non-reactive. Which molecular diagnostic test is most likely to confirm the etiology?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Targeted gene sequencing for GAA repeat expansions in the FXN gene

options.label: B
options.text: Polymerase chain reaction for CAG repeat expansion in huntingtin gene

options.label: C
options.text: Multiplex ligation probe amplification for PMP22 duplication

options.label: D
options.text: Southern blot analysis for CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene

options.label: E
options.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization for deletion on chromosome 22q11

explanation: This patient presents with classic Friedreich ataxia: combination of dorsal column loss (sensory ataxia), corticospinal involvement (extensor plantars), peripheral neuropathy (absent DTRs), and skeletal abnormalities (pes cavus). Testing for GAA repeat expansion in the FXN gene (encoding frataxin) on chromosome 9 confirms the diagnosis. Normal cobalamin rules out subacute combined degeneration, and negative RPR rules out tabes dorsalis.
high_yield_pearl: Friedreich ataxia is confirmed by detecting GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FXN gene on chromosome 9.

stem: A 14-year-old boy presents with progressive morning headaches, vomiting, upward gaze paralysis, convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upward gaze, and bilateral pupillary light-near dissociation (pupils constrict to accommodation but do not react to direct light). Brain MRI reveals a 2.5-cm mass in the pineal gland compressing the dorsal midbrain. What specific anatomical structure compression produces this constellation of neuro-ophthalmic findings (Parinaud syndrome)?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Midbrain tectum including superior colliculi and pretectal nuclei

options.label: B
options.text: Ventral tegmentum including oculomotor nerve roots in the interpeduncular fossa

options.label: C
options.text: Abducens nucleus within the facial colliculus of the dorsal pontine floor

options.label: D
options.text: Lateral geniculate body within the posterior inferior thalamic complex

options.label: E
options.text: Medial longitudinal fasciculus traversing the paramedian midbrain core

explanation: Parinaud syndrome (dorsal midbrain syndrome) is caused by compression of the midbrain tectum (specifically the pretectal area and superior colliculi), most commonly by a pineal region tumor (germinoma or pineocytoma/pineoblastoma) or obstructive hydrocephalus. Features include upward gaze palsy (compression of vertical gaze center in rostral interstitial nucleus of MLF/pretectal area), convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation, and bilateral eyelid retraction (Collier sign).
high_yield_pearl: Parinaud syndrome results from pineal mass compression of the dorsal midbrain tectum (pretectal area and superior colliculi), causing upward gaze palsy and light-near dissociation.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is evaluated for secondary amenorrhea and spontaneous bilateral galactorrhea. Contrast MRI of the sella reveals an 8-mm non-calcified microadenoma within the adenohypophysis, and her serum prolactin is 240 ng/mL (normal <25 ng/mL). She is started on cabergoline therapy. What is the molecular mechanism of action by which this medication causes rapid reduction in prolactin secretion and tumor volume?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Stimulation of pituitary dopamine D2 receptors coupled to inhibitory G-protein Gi

options.label: B
options.text: Competitive antagonism at nuclear estrogen and progesterone receptor complexes

options.label: C
options.text: Direct blockade of voltage-gated L-type calcium channels on anterior lactotrophs

options.label: D
options.text: Inhibition of somatostatin receptor subtype 2 on hypothalamic releasing cells

options.label: E
options.text: Antagonism of prolactin releasing hormone receptors within the hypophyseal portal

explanation: Prolactinomas are benign lactotroph adenomas of the anterior pituitary. Dopamine (prolactin-inhibiting factor) released by the hypothalamus normally inhibits prolactin synthesis and secretion via dopamine D2 receptors coupled to Gi proteins (adenylyl cyclase inhibition). Cabergoline and bromocriptine are potent dopamine D2 receptor agonists that mimic this tonic inhibition, suppressing prolactin secretion and inducing shrinkage of lactotroph tumors.
high_yield_pearl: Dopamine D2 receptor agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine) inhibit prolactin secretion and reduce tumor size in prolactinomas via Gi signaling.

stem: A 44-year-old man with uncorrected tetralogy of Fallot presents with high fever, dull headache, and new-onset focal motor seizures. Brain MRI demonstrates a single well-circumscribed ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe with marked surrounding vasogenic edema. Stereotactic aspiration yields purulent fluid growing Streptococcus viridans and peptostreptococci. Why did his congenital cardiac defect predispose him to this localized intracranial pyogenic infection?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Right-to-left cardiac shunt bypassing pulmonary alveolar capillary filtration

options.label: B
options.text: Chronic systemic venous hypertension causing retrograde venous microinfarcts

options.label: C
