options.label: D
options.text: Chronic hypoxemia selectively impairing polymorphonuclear phagocytosis

options.label: E
options.text: Direct communication between cardiac chambers and the azygos venous drainage

explanation: Normally, bacteria that enter the venous circulation (e.g., from dental procedures or oral mucosa) are filtered and phagocytosed by pulmonary alveolar macrophages and capillaries. In patients with cyanotic congenital heart disease and right-to-left shunts (such as tetralogy of Fallot or Eisenmenger syndrome), venous blood bypasses the pulmonary filter, allowing transient bacteremia to seed the cerebral circulation, predisposing to brain abscesses.
high_yield_pearl: Right-to-left cardiac shunts bypass pulmonary capillary filtration, allowing transient bacteremia to seed the brain and form abscesses.

stem: A 34-year-old man exhibits an intention tremor, past-pointing on finger-to-nose testing, and impaired rapid alternating hand movements on the right side only. Strength and sensation are completely intact bilaterally. A focal lesion is identified in the right deep cerebellum. Which deep nucleus and output peduncle are responsible for these motor planning deficits?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Dentate nucleus projecting via the superior peduncle

options.label: B
options.text: Fastigial nucleus projecting via the inferior peduncle

options.label: C
options.text: Emboliform nucleus projecting via the middle peduncle

options.label: D
options.text: Globose nucleus projecting via the stria medullaris

options.label: E
options.text: Interposed nucleus projecting via the dorsal column

explanation: The lateral cerebellar hemisphere coordinates multi-joint voluntary limb movements and motor planning through the dentate nucleus. Dentate efferents exit through the superior cerebellar peduncle (brachium conjunctivum), decussate in the lower midbrain to reach the contralateral ventrolateral (VL) thalamus, and project to motor cortex. Corticospinal fibers then cross back at the medullary decussation, resulting in ipsilateral cerebellar deficits.
high_yield_pearl: The lateral cerebrocerebellar hemisphere projects via the dentate nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle to coordinate ipsilateral limb motor planning.

stem: A respiratory therapist performs emergent endotracheal intubation on a patient with fulminant Neisseria meningitidis meningitis during which she is directly exposed to respiratory droplets without eye or face protection. What chemoprophylactic regimen and corresponding mechanism of action are indicated to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage in this exposed healthcare worker?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Rifampin via inhibition of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase transcription

options.label: B
options.text: Amoxicillin via inhibition of transpeptidase-mediated peptidoglycan crosslinking

options.label: C
options.text: Azithromycin via reversible binding to the 50S bacterial ribosomal subunit

options.label: D
options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole via sequential block of folate enzymatic synthesis

options.label: E
options.text: Doxycycline via binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit preventing tRNA docking

explanation: Close contacts of patients with invasive meningococcal disease (including healthcare workers with direct respiratory droplet exposure) require chemoprophylaxis to eradicate nasopharyngeal colonization. First-line prophylaxis is oral rifampin (which inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase) for 2 days. Single-dose ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone IM are alternative regimens.
high_yield_pearl: Meningococcal close-contact chemoprophylaxis is achieved with rifampin (DNA-dependent RNA polymerase inhibitor), ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents with severe lancinating pain deep within his right ear canal, followed three days later by a vesicular rash on the right external auditory concha, complete right-sided facial weakness including the forehead, and vertigo with horizontal nystagmus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome). Reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus within which sensory ganglion accounts for this clinical syndrome?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve within the petrous temporal bone

options.label: B
options.text: Trigeminal semilunar ganglion located in the floor of the middle cranial fossa

options.label: C
options.text: Spiral ganglion located within the modiolus of the bony cochlear canal

options.label: D
options.text: Superior jugular ganglion of the glossopharyngeal nerve at the foramen

options.label: E
options.text: Ciliary parasympathetic ganglion situated in the posterior orbital apex

explanation: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus) is caused by reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in the geniculate ganglion of cranial nerve VII. The viral spread causes painful vesicular eruption in the external auditory canal and concha (sensory branch of CN VII), peripheral facial nerve palsy (including forehead), and vestibulocochlear symptoms (vertigo, tinnitus, sensorineural hearing loss) due to proximity of CN VIII.
high_yield_pearl: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is caused by VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of CN VII, causing ear vesicles, facial palsy, and vestibulocochlear symptoms.

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with progressive morning headaches, vomiting, severe truncal instability, and downbeat nystagmus. When seated with his back fully supported against a wall, his finger-to-nose coordination and rapid alternating movements are completely normal. Neuroimaging reveals a mass invading the cerebellar vermis and roof of the fourth ventricle. Which functional division and deep nucleus are primary sites of compression?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Vestibulocerebellar flocculonodular lobe and fastigial nucleus

options.label: B
options.text: Cerebrocerebellar lateral hemisphere and dentate projection nucleus

options.label: C
options.text: Spinocerebellar intermediate hemisphere and emboliform nucleus

options.label: D
options.text: Paleocerebellar paralaminar cortex and globose projection nucleus

options.label: E
options.text: Neocerebellar ventral cortex and lateral vestibular nucleus complex

explanation: Midline cerebellar lesions (such as medulloblastoma) compress the vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe and vermis) and the fastigial nucleus. This results in truncal ataxia, titubation, dysequilibrium, and downbeat nystagmus, while sparing appendicular coordination (lateral hemisphere/dentate), so limb testing remains intact when trunk support is provided.
high_yield_pearl: Vermis and flocculonodular lobe lesions cause truncal ataxia, dysequilibrium, and nystagmus with preserved limb coordination when the trunk is supported.

stem: A 63-year-old man presents with rapid cognitive decline, personality changes, and morning headaches over four weeks. Brain MRI shows a solitary 4.5-cm rim-enhancing frontotemporal mass crossing the corpus callosum with extensive surrounding vasogenic edema. Histopathology confirms a Grade 4 astrocytoma with pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation. Molecular testing reveals hypermethylation of the O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) gene promoter. What is the clinical significance of this epigenetic alteration?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Enhanced tumor susceptibility and improved response to temozolomide chemotherapy

options.label: B
options.text: Resistance to ionizing radiation therapy requiring high-dose stereotactic surgery

options.label: C
options.text: Significantly elevated risk of leptomeningeal dissemination along spinal cord

options.label: D
options.text: Rapid loss of heterozygosity in the neurofibromatosis tumor suppressor gene

options.label: E
options.text: Constitutive vascular endothelial growth factor overexpression and hemorrhage

explanation: In glioblastoma (GBM), MGMT promoter hypermethylation silences the MGMT DNA-repair enzyme, which would otherwise remove alkyl adducts created by temozolomide. Silencing MGMT prevents tumor cells from repairing alkylating chemotherapy damage, conferring significantly improved sensitivity to temozolomide and better overall survival.
high_yield_pearl: MGMT promoter methylation silences DNA repair in glioblastoma, conferring increased sensitivity to temozolomide and improved survival.

stem: A 26-year-old woman is admitted to the continuous video-EEG monitoring unit for evaluation of daily drug-resistant seizures. During an observed episode, she exhibits asynchronous, out-of-phase thrashing of all four limbs, forceful pelvic thrusting, side-to-side head shaking, and tightly closed eyes that actively resist manual opening by the examiner. Concurrent continuous electroencephalography shows a normal posterior dominant alpha rhythm with muscle artifact and no epileptiform discharges. Which physical examination sign during an episode is most specific for psychogenic non-epileptic seizures?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Active resistance to forced passive eye opening with forceful eyelid closure

options.label: B
options.text: Presence of bilateral plantar extensor responses immediately after the event

options.label: C
options.text: Transient elevation of serum prolactin measured twenty minutes post-ictus

options.label: D
options.text: Lateral tongue biting along the border of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue

options.label: E
options.text: Development of postictal stertorous snoring breathing with metabolic lactic acidosis

explanation: Psychogenic Non-Epileptic Seizures (PNES) are functional neurological disorders mimicking epilepsy. Key semiological signs include out-of-phase limb movements, pelvic thrusting, head shaking ('no-no' motions), preserved consciousness during bilateral movements, absence of postictal confusion, and crucially, forced eyelid closure with active resistance to examiner opening (epileptic seizures typically feature open eyes). Normal EEG during an active event confirms the non-epileptic nature.
high_yield_pearl: PNES is characterized by active resistance to eye opening, pelvic thrusting, out-of-phase movements, and normal concurrent EEG without postictal prolactin surge.

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents with acute vertigo, vomiting, right-sided peripheral facial paralysis involving her forehead and lower face, right sensorineural hearing loss, right Horner syndrome, right appendicular limb ataxia, and loss of pain and temperature on her right face and left body. What distinct clinical findings conclusively differentiate this lateral pontine syndrome from a lateral medullary syndrome?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy and sensorineural hearing loss

options.label: B
options.text: Severe dysphagia, dysarthria, and deviation of the uvula away from the lesion

options.label: C
options.text: Contralateral loss of vibration and joint position sense in the limbs

options.label: D
options.text: Ipsilateral deviation of the tongue with muscular atrophy and fasciculations

options.label: E
options.text: Contralateral flaccid hemiparesis sparing the upper and lower face

explanation: Lateral pontine syndrome is caused by occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), whereas lateral medullary syndrome is caused by PICA. Both share Horner syndrome, cerebellar ataxia, and crossed pain/temperature loss. The crucial distinguishing features of AICA (pons) are damage to the facial nucleus (CN VII: ipsilateral full-face paralysis) and cochlear nuclei/internal auditory artery (CN VIII: ipsilateral sensorineural deafness). In contrast, PICA (medulla) damages nucleus ambiguus (CN IX/X: hoarseness, dysphagia).
high_yield_pearl: AICA (lateral pontine) stroke features ipsilateral facial paralysis and hearing loss; PICA (lateral medullary) stroke features hoarseness, dysphagia, and no facial paralysis.

stem: A 16-year-old girl is evaluated for worsening clumsiness and progressive gait unsteadiness over two years. Physical examination shows bilateral pes cavus, hammer toes, severe thoracic kyphoscoliosis, absent lower extremity deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral upward Babinski signs. What underlying cardiac pathology represents the primary cause of premature death in patients with this disorder?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with asymmetric septal hypertrophy

options.label: B
options.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy secondary to chronic viral myocarditis

options.label: C
options.text: Fibromuscular dysplasia involving proximal coronary arteries

options.label: D
options.text: Myxomatous mitral valve prolapse with chordal rupture

options.label: E
options.text: Constrictive pericarditis with progressive fibrocalcification

explanation: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FXN gene on chromosome 9, encoding frataxin. Frataxin deficiency impairs mitochondrial iron homeostasis and respiration. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (asymmetric septal hypertrophy and arrhythmia) occurs in >90% of patients and is the leading cause of death.
high_yield_pearl: Friedreich ataxia (GAA repeat in FXN) presents with spinocerebellar ataxia, absent DTRs, extensor plantars, pes cavus, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (leading cause of death).

stem: A 44-year-old man develops rapidly progressive symmetric leg weakness and difficulty climbing stairs 3 weeks after an episode of bloody diarrhea. Physical examination shows flaccid quadriparesis and generalized areflexia, but sensation is intact. Nerve conduction studies show markedly reduced compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes with preserved conduction velocities and normal distal latencies. What is the molecular target of the autoantibodies driving this presentation?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Schwann cell peripheral myelin protein 22 located in compact internodal myelin

options.label: B
options.text: GM1 and GD1a gangliosides localized at the axolemma of motor nodes of Ranvier

options.label: C
options.text: GQ1b gangliosides concentrated within the oculomotor and abducens nerve sheaths

options.label: D
options.text: Postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors situated at the motor endplate

options.label: E
options.text: Presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels at the neuromuscular junction

explanation: This patient has the acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome, classic following Campylobacter jejuni enteritis. Lipooligosaccharides on C. jejuni share molecular mimicry with gangliosides GM1 and GD1a. Antibodies bind directly to the axolemma at the nodes of Ranvier, recruiting complement and macrophages that disrupt voltage-gated sodium channels. This produces pure motor axonal injury characterized electrodiagnostically by reduced CMAP amplitudes without conduction slowing or prolonged latencies.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 29-year-old man successfully undergoes resection of a cerebellar hemangioblastoma. His family pedigree reveals that his father died of bilateral kidney cancer at age 42, and his paternal aunt was treated for a retinal angioma. Genetic testing confirms a pathogenic germline deletion in the VHL tumor suppressor gene. In addition to periodic brain and spinal cord MRI, what annual surveillance modality is critical to detect the most frequent cause of cancer mortality in this syndrome?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Abdominal MRI or contrast-enhanced ultrasound to screen for renal cell carcinoma

options.label: B
options.text: High-resolution chest computed tomography to evaluate for pulmonary hamartomas

options.label: C
options.text: Annual colonoscopy beginning at age thirty to resect adenomatous polyps

options.label: D
options.text: Serum calcitonin and thyroid ultrasound screening for medullary thyroid cancer

options.label: E
options.text: Endoscopic ultrasound to evaluate for diffuse gastric adenocarcinoma

explanation: Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is an autosomal dominant condition (deletion on chromosome 3p) that predisposes to cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC), pheochromocytomas, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. Renal cell carcinoma is bilateral/multifocal and represents the leading cause of mortality in VHL patients. Annual abdominal imaging (MRI or ultrasound) is recommended starting in early adulthood.
high_yield_pearl: VHL syndrome (chromosome 3p) requires regular abdominal surveillance for clear cell renal cell carcinoma (the leading cause of death) and pheochromocytoma.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with stereotyped episodes beginning with a rising epigastric sensation ('butterflies in stomach') and intense déjà vu, followed by motionless blank staring, lip smacking, right-hand picking automatisms, and ninety seconds of unresponsiveness with postictal amnesia. Coronal T2-weighted MRI shows right hippocampal atrophy and hyperintensity. What is the classic histopathologic finding in this resected hippocampal tissue?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Marked pyramidal neuronal loss with dense fibrillary astrogliosis in CA1 and CA4

options.label: B
options.text: Extensive neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau proteins

options.label: C
options.text: Intracellular Lewy bodies containing aggregated alpha-synuclein polymers

options.label: D
options.text: Perivascular lymphohistiocytic cuffing with viral Cowdry A inclusion bodies

options.label: E
options.text: Widespread cortical microvacuolation and spongiform neuronal degeneration

explanation: This patient has mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE), the most common refractory focal epilepsy syndrome in adults, characterized by epigastric auras, autonomic/psychic sensations, automatisms, and impaired awareness. The underlying etiology is hippocampal sclerosis (mesial temporal sclerosis), histologically characterized by selective neuronal loss and dense astrogliosis in the Sommer sector (CA1), end-folium (CA4), and dentate gyrus, with relative sparing of CA2.
high_yield_pearl: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy is caused by hippocampal sclerosis, characterized by neuronal loss and astrogliosis in hippocampal CA1/CA4 subfields.

stem: A student compares a patient who achieves full motor recovery after severe Guillain-Barre syndrome to a patient who remains paraplegic after spinal cord multiple sclerosis. Which physiological difference between central and peripheral nervous system environments primarily explains why central remyelination fails following injury?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Central oligodendrocytes completely lack the metabolic machinery to synthesize galactocerebroside

options.label: B
options.text: CNS myelin debris and astrocytic glial scars express potent inhibitors of axonal outgrowth and remyelination

options.label: C
options.text: Schwann cells are permanently immune-privileged and cannot be recognized by circulating cytotoxic T-cells

options.label: D
options.text: The blood-brain barrier permanently excludes glucose and ATP from injured central axon cylinders

options.label: E
options.text: Peripheral axons are entirely unmyelinated and do not require neuroglial sheath replacement after trauma

explanation: In the PNS, Schwann cells readily proliferate, express neurotrophic factors, produce a basement membrane rich in laminin, and macrophages rapidly clear myelin debris, permitting vigorous remyelination. In the CNS, remyelination is severely impeded because central myelin debris contains potent neurite outgrowth inhibitors (Nogo-A, MAG, OMgp), microglial clearance is slow, and reactive astrocytes form a dense chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan-rich glial scar that physically blocks oligodendrocyte precursor migration and remyelination.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with progressive bilateral hearing loss and recurrent unsteadiness. Brain MRI demonstrates bilateral enhancing masses in the cerebellopontine angles expanding both internal acoustic meatuses, as well as multiple dural-based parietal convex masses with dural tails. Genetic testing reveals a heterozygous inactivating mutation in a tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 22q12. What is the fundamental physiological role of the protein encoded by this gene?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Linking the actin cytoskeleton to cell-surface contact-inhibition proteins

options.label: B
options.text: Binding free cytoplasmic iron to prevent generation of hydroxyl radicals

options.label: C
options.text: Hydrolyzing epidermal growth factor receptor extracellular domains

options.label: D
options.text: Catalyzing DNA double-strand break repair via homologous recombination

options.label: E
options.text: Ubiquitinating cytosolic oncoproteins to trigger proteasomal destruction

explanation: Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2) is caused by mutations on chromosome 22q12 in the NF2 gene encoding merlin (schwannomin). Merlin is a member of the ERM (ezrin-radixin-moesin) protein family that links actin cytoskeleton to cell membrane glycoproteins (such as CD44) to mediate contact inhibition of cell growth. Deficiency of merlin causes multiple schwannomas (characteristically bilateral vestibular schwannomas), meningiomas, and ependymomas (MISME syndrome).
high_yield_pearl: NF2 (chromosome 22q) encodes merlin, a cytoskeletal scaffolding protein mediating contact inhibition; loss causes bilateral acoustic schwannomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas.

stem: A 61-year-old man presents with acute double vision and weakness. Neurological examination reveals complete left-sided peripheral facial weakness involving the upper and lower face (cranial nerve VII), inability to abduct the left eye beyond the midline (cranial nerve VI), and dense contralateral right-sided hemiplegia (corticospinal tract). Sensation across all modalities is completely preserved. What alternating ventral brainstem stroke syndrome does this constellation represent?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Millard-Gubler syndrome caused by an ischemic infarct in the ventrolateral pons

options.label: B
options.text: Wallenberg syndrome caused by an ischemic infarct in the dorsolateral medulla

options.label: C
options.text: Weber syndrome caused by an ischemic infarct in the ventral midbrain peduncle

options.label: D
options.text: Benedikt syndrome caused by an ischemic infarct in the dorsal midbrain tegmentum

options.label: E
options.text: Foville syndrome caused by an ischemic infarct in the dorsal rostral midbrain

explanation: Millard-Gubler syndrome (ventral pontine syndrome) is an alternating hemiplegia caused by occlusion of circumferential or paramedian branches of the basilar artery. The lesion affects the ventral caudal pons, damaging: 1) exiting fibers of CN VI (ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy), 2) exiting fibers of CN VII (ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy), and 3) the corticospinal tract (contralateral hemiplegia). Sensory tracts (spinothalamic, medial lemniscus) lie more dorsally and are spared.
high_yield_pearl: Millard-Gubler syndrome (ventral pontine stroke) presents with ipsilateral CN VI and CN VII palsies and contralateral hemiplegia, sparing sensation.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents following an unprovoked generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Non-contrast head CT reveals a well-demarcated cortical mass in the right frontal lobe with coarse intrinsic calcifications. Histopathological examination shows monomorphic round cells with clear perinuclear halos ('fried-egg' appearance) embedded in a network of branching delicate capillaries ('chicken-wire' pattern). Cytogenetic analysis demonstrates complete whole-arm co-deletion of chromosomes 1p and 19q. What is the clinical implication of this chromosomal finding?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Marked therapeutic sensitivity to alkylating chemotherapy and favorable prognosis

options.label: B
options.text: High resistance to radiotherapy and rapid dedifferentiation to glioblastoma

options.label: C
options.text: Predisposition to aggressive multicentric metastases outside the neuroaxis

options.label: D
options.text: Contraindication to gross total surgical resection due to high bleeding risk

options.label: E
options.text: Need for emergent bilateral optic nerve decompression to prevent blindness

explanation: Oligodendrogliomas are defined molecularly by IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion (formed by an unbalanced translocation t(1;19)(q10;p10)). The 1p/19q codeletion confers exquisite sensitivity to procarbazine-CCNU-vincristine (PCV) and temozolomide chemotherapy, and is associated with significantly longer overall survival.
high_yield_pearl: Oligodendrogliomas have 'fried-egg' cells, 'chicken-wire' vessels, calcifications, and 1p/19q codeletion predicting chemosensitivity and prolonged survival.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with horizontal diplopia. On neurological examination, during attempted leftward conjugate gaze, the right eye fails to adduct past the midline, and the left abducting eye exhibits horizontal nystagmus. However, when the patient focuses on an approaching target at the nose, both eyes converge symmetrically and both pupils constrict. Which anatomical feature explains the preservation of adduction during convergence?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Convergence pathways travel exclusively through the contralateral abducens nucleus

options.label: B
options.text: Convergence signals project directly from pretectal inputs to the oculomotor nucleus bypassing the MLF

options.label: C
options.text: Convergence relies on cortical innervation from the frontal eye fields traveling in the pyramid

options.label: D
options.text: The medial longitudinal fasciculus only carries autonomic pupillary fibers from the midbrain

options.label: E
options.text: The abducens motor neurons provide primary innervation to the medial rectus during near fixation

explanation: This patient has right internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) due to a demyelinating lesion of the right medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). Conjugate horizontal saccades require abducens interneurons in the pons to send axons through the contralateral MLF to the oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain. In contrast, the vergence pathway arises in the visual association cortex and midbrain pretectal area, projecting directly to both oculomotor nuclear complexes without traversing the MLF. Thus, convergence and pupillary near-response are preserved.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 62-year-old man with a twenty-year history of poorly controlled hypertension develops sudden right-sided weakness. Neurological examination reveals complete, symmetrical motor hemiparesis equally affecting his right face, arm, and leg (3/5 strength throughout) with brisk reflexes and a right extensor plantar sign. Sensation to all modalities, visual fields, and language are completely intact. What microvascular pathology in which deep brain structure is responsible for this classic pure motor stroke?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Lipohyalinosis of lenticulostriate arteries in the posterior limb of capsule

options.label: B
options.text: Atheroembolism of anterior choroidal artery to the lateral geniculate nucleus

options.label: C
options.text: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm rupture within the medial thalamic nucleus

options.label: D
options.text: Fibrinoid necrosis of basilar circumferential branches in the dorsal pons

options.label: E
options.text: Thromboembolism of the Heubner artery into the anterior internal capsule

explanation: Pure motor hemiparesis is the most common lacunar stroke syndrome (>50%), resulting from ischemic infarction of the posterior limb of the internal capsule (carrying descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers). The underlying microvascular pathology is lipohyalinosis and microatheroma of the deep penetrating lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery, driven by chronic systemic hypertension.
high_yield_pearl: Pure motor lacunar stroke is caused by lipohyalinosis of lenticulostriate arteries, selectively damaging the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

stem: A 30-year-old HIV-infected man with a CD4 count of 45/uL presents with headaches and left-sided hemiparesis. Contrast brain MRI reveals multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema located predominantly at the basal ganglia and corticomedullary junction. Serum IgG antibodies to Toxoplasma gondii are positive. What is the standard initial clinical management strategy?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Empiric pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin with repeat imaging in 14 days

options.label: B
options.text: Emergent stereotactic brain biopsy prior to initiating any antimicrobial therapy

options.label: C
options.text: Whole-brain radiation therapy combined with high-dose intravenous methotrexate

options.label: D
options.text: Intravenous ganciclovir monotherapy directed against cytomegalovirus encephalitis

options.label: E
options.text: Surgical craniotomy and evacuation of all ring-enhancing purulent abscesses

explanation: In an HIV patient with CD4 < 100/uL presenting with multiple ring-enhancing lesions and positive Toxoplasma IgG, the presumptive diagnosis is cerebral toxoplasmosis. The standard approach is an empiric trial of pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin (folinic acid to prevent bone marrow suppression). Clinical and radiologic response is expected within 10-14 days. If lesions enlarge or fail to respond, stereotactic biopsy is indicated to evaluate for primary CNS lymphoma.
high_yield_pearl: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in AIDS with CD4 < 100 warrant empiric pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin; biopsy is reserved for non-responders.

stem: A 28-year-old agricultural worker from rural Latin America presents with new-onset generalized seizures. Brain MRI shows multiple small cystic parenchymal lesions, including viable cysts with an eccentric mural nodule (representing an invaginated scolex) and multiple calcified granulomas. Through which transmission route did this patient acquire this neuroparasitic infection?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Fecal-oral ingestion of Taenia solium eggs shed in the stool of a human tapeworm carrier

options.label: B
options.text: Ingestion of undercooked pork contaminated with encysted larval Taenia solium cysticerci

options.label: C
options.text: Direct percutaneous penetration by cercarial larvae swimming in freshwater irrigation

options.label: D
options.text: Inhalation of infective embryonated ova carried in contaminated barnyard dust

options.label: E
options.text: Bite of an infected reduviid bug defecating near the primary skin puncture wound

explanation: Neurocysticercosis is caused by ingestion of Taenia solium eggs via fecal-oral contamination from a human carrier of the adult intestinal tapeworm. Once ingested, oncospheres hatch, penetrate intestinal mucosa, and hematogenously spread to the brain (forming cystic lesions with a scolex). In contrast, eating undercooked pork containing larval cysticerci causes intestinal tapeworm infection (taeniasis), NOT cysticercosis.
high_yield_pearl: Neurocysticercosis is caused by fecal-oral ingestion of Taenia solium eggs from human stool (eating contaminated undercooked pork causes adult intestinal taeniasis).

stem: A 52-year-old accountant recovers from surgical resection of a right cerebellar hemisphere hemangioblastoma. While his motor coordination recovers completely, his family notes striking changes: he exhibits concrete thinking, severe planning deficits, flattened affect, and impaired verbal fluency. Neuropsychological evaluation confirms Cerebellar Cognitive Affective Syndrome. Through which thalamic relay does the neocerebellum normally communicate with prefrontal cortex to support these executive functions?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Ventrolateral and mediodorsal nuclei of the contralateral thalamus

options.label: B
options.text: Ventral posteromedial nucleus carrying facial sensory information

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral geniculate nucleus mediating visual spatial attention

options.label: D
options.text: Medial geniculate body coordinating auditory working memory

options.label: E
options.text: Anterior thalamic nucleus coordinating mamillothalamic memory circuits

explanation: The posterior neocerebellar lobes connect reciprocally with the prefrontal cortex via the dentatothalamocortical pathway, synapsing in the ventrolateral (VL) and mediodorsal (MD) thalamic nuclei. Lesions here cause Cerebellar Cognitive Affective Syndrome (Schmahmann syndrome), presenting with executive dysfunction, spatial cognition deficits, personality change/blunting, and language impairment.
high_yield_pearl: The posterior neocerebellum projects via the dentate nucleus to ventrolateral and mediodorsal thalamic nuclei to regulate executive cognitive functions and affect.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with progressive limb unsteadiness and persistent headaches. Routine laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 19.8 g/dL and hematocrit of 59%. Brain MRI reveals a highly vascular cystic lesion with an enhancing mural nodule in the cerebellar hemisphere. Histology reveals lipid-rich foamy stromal cells interspersed among extensive thin-walled capillary networks. What molecular mechanism directly links his underlying genetic defect to the erythrocytosis?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Impaired degradation of hypoxia-inducible factor driving erythropoietin

options.label: B
options.text: Constitutive hyperactivation of fibroblast growth factor receptor kinase

options.label: C
options.text: Direct somatic mutation in the erythropoietin receptor promoter region

options.label: D

options.label: E

The VHL tumor suppressor protein forms part of an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1alpha) for proteasomal degradation under normoxic conditions. Loss of VHL causes constitutive HIF-1alpha accumulation, driving transcription of VEGF, PDGF, and erythropoietin (EPO), resulting in paraneoplastic secondary polycythemia.
high_yield_pearl: VHL mutations prevent ubiquitin-mediated degradation of HIF-1alpha, driving VEGF and EPO transcription, leading to hemangioblastomas and secondary polycythemia.

stem: An experimental neurophysiology protocol selectively microinjects a GABA-A receptor agonist into the interposed nuclei (emboliform and globose) of non-human primates. Which physiological motor deficit is selectively elicited during ongoing voluntary target-directed limb movements?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Impaired real-time execution and error correction of limb trajectories

options.label: B
options.text: Severe resting tremor that completely abolishes upon voluntary initiation

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.label: E

explanation: The intermediate cerebellar hemisphere (spinocerebellum) projects to the interposed nuclei (emboliform and globose). Unlike the dentate nucleus (which handles motor planning prior to movement), the interposed nuclei project to the red nucleus and motor cortex to regulate ongoing movement execution and correct ongoing movement trajectory errors.
high_yield_pearl: The interposed nuclei (emboliform and globose) receive spinocerebellar input and modulate ongoing voluntary limb movement execution and trajectory correction.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents with progressive difficulty walking, frequent ankle sprains, and bilateral foot deformities since early adolescence. Examination shows high arching of the foot (pes cavus), claw toes, atrophy of the intrinsic foot muscles and distal calves ("stork leg" appearance), and bilateral absent ankle reflexes. Sural nerve biopsy reveals prominent "onion-bulb" formations. What is the genetic mechanism responsible for this autosomal dominant condition?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Trinucleotide GAA repeat expansion in the first intron of the frataxin gene

options.label: B
options.text: Duplication of a 1.4-megabase segment containing the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17p11.2

options.label: C

explanation: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A (CMT1A) is the most common hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and caused by a 1.4-Mb duplication on chromosome 17p11.2 encompassing the peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) gene. PMP22 overexpression disrupts compact myelin maintenance, leading to repeated cycles of demyelination and remyelination that produce redundant concentric Schwann cell cytoplasmic layers resembling 'onion bulbs' on biopsy.

stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with hyperacute fever, bifrontal headache, vomiting, and photophobia four days after diving into a warm freshwater lake in Texas during mid-July. Lumbar puncture demonstrates a marked neutrophilic pleocytosis, severe hypoglycorrhachia, and motile amoebic trophozoites on a fresh wet mount. By which anatomical route did this free-living amoeba gain access to the subarachnoid space?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Cribriform plate perforations alongside the olfactory nerve fila

options.label: B
options.text: Hematogenous seeding across the blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier

options.label: C

options.label: D

high_yield_pearl: Naegleria fowleri penetrates the nasal olfactory mucosa and traverses the cribriform plate to cause fatal primary amoebic meningoencephalitis.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is evaluated for subacute gait unsteadiness and sensory loss. Lumbar puncture is performed. Which of the following cerebrospinal fluid findings would most strongly argue AGAINST a primary diagnosis of multiple sclerosis and point toward an active infectious process?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Presence of five distinct oligoclonal immunoglobulin G bands absent in matched serum

options.label: B
options.text: Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis of 14 leukocytes per microliter with normal glucose

options.label: C
options.text: Marked neutrophilic pleocytosis of 850 cells per microliter with a CSF to serum glucose ratio of 0.25

options.label: D
options.text: Moderately elevated cerebrospinal fluid immunoglobulin G index of 0.85

options.label: E
options.text: Total cerebrospinal fluid protein concentration of 55 milligrams per deciliter

A marked neutrophilic pleocytosis (>500-1000 cells/uL) with hypoglycorrhachia (CSF:serum glucose <0.4) is virtually never seen in MS and strongly indicates acute bacterial, fungal, or tuberculous meningitis.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 44-year-old man presents with a slow-growing, painful mass in his left posterior thigh along the trajectory of the sciatic nerve. During surgical excision, the surgeon notes that the mass is well-circumscribed, encapsulated, and lies eccentric to the main nerve trunk, allowing complete enucleation without sacrificing functional nerve fascicles. Histopathology reveals alternating Antoni A and B areas with intense S100 positivity. What surgical and pathological feature fundamentally distinguishes this tumor from a localized neurofibroma?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: True fibrous encapsulation and eccentric displacement of intact nerve fascicles

options.label: B
options.text: Absence of S100 immunoreactivity within neoplastic supporting stromal cells

options.label: C
options.text: Diffuse infiltrative entrapment of nerve fibers necessitating complete transection

options.label: D
options.text: Origin from central oligodendrocytes rather than peripheral neural crest cells

options.label: E
options.text: High malignant transformation rate exceeding fifty percent during adulthood

explanation: Schwannomas are true encapsulated tumors that grow eccentrically from a single nerve fascicle, pushing the remaining nerve fibers aside without infiltrating them; thus, they can usually be resected while sparing the nerve trunk. In contrast, neurofibromas lack a capsule, infiltrate and entangle multiple nerve fascicles directly (making nerve-sparing resection impossible), and have a higher risk of malignant transformation (especially in plexiform neurofibromas in NF1).
high_yield_pearl: Schwannomas are encapsulated and grow eccentrically from a nerve without fascicular infiltration, allowing nerve-sparing surgical enucleation.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with fever, lethargy, confusion, ataxia, and new-onset seizures 10 days after recovering from a viral upper respiratory illness. Brain MRI reveals widespread, bilateral, asymmetric, poorly demarcated hyperintensities in the subcortical white matter and deep basal ganglia, all demonstrating homogeneous gadolinium enhancement. Which feature most reliably differentiates this condition from multiple sclerosis?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Detection of elevated cerebrospinal fluid protein concentration above 100 mg/dL

options.label: B
options.text: Monophasic course with simultaneous inflammatory lesions of identical chronological age and encephalopathy

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of multiple white matter lesions involving the posterior fossa and spinal cord

options.label: D
options.text: Favorable clinical improvement following a short course of high-dose corticosteroids

options.label: E
options.text: Development of focal neurological motor deficits affecting the appendicular musculature

explanation: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) is a post-infectious, immune-mediated demyelinating encephalopathy primarily affecting children. Unlike multiple sclerosis, which requires dissemination in time and space with lesions of varying ages (some enhancing, some non-enhancing), ADEM is characteristically monophasic, features prominent early encephalopathy (lethargy, delirium, coma), and shows multifocal lesions that are all of identical age (all enhancing simultaneously on MRI).
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with severe suboccipital throbbing headaches worsened by coughing and sneezing, downbeat nystagmus, and progressive bilateral hand muscle wasting with loss of pinprick and temperature sensation across her shoulders and arms. Brain MRI confirms 8 mm herniation of cerebellar tonsils below the foramen magnum. What spinal cord finding is most likely present?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.text: Central fluid-filled syringomyelia cavity in cervical cord

options.label: B
options.text: Extensive demyelination isolated to the dorsal funiculi

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Extramedullary schwannoma compressing the lumbar thecal sac

options.label: E

explanation: Chiari I malformation is characterized by downward herniation of cerebellar tonsils (>5 mm) through the foramen magnum, often asymptomatic until adulthood. It disrupts normal CSF flow dynamics at the craniocervical junction, strongly associating with cervical syringomyelia. Syringomyelia expands to compress anterior white commissure fibers, producing a 'cape-like' loss of pain and temperature sensation.
high_yield_pearl: Chiari I malformation (tonsillar ectopia >5 mm) commonly presents in young adults with cough headaches, downbeat nystagmus, and syringomyelia (cape-like thermoanalgesia).

stem: An 8-year-old girl is evaluated for morning nausea, vomiting, and progressive right-sided clumsiness. Posterior fossa MRI reveals a large cystic mass with an intensely enhancing mural nodule in the right cerebellar hemisphere. Following surgical resection, histopathology demonstrates biphasic tissue composed of bipolar piloid astrocytes with hair-like processes, eosinophilic Rosenthal fibers, and granular bodies. Which molecular alteration is most commonly the primary genetic driver of this neoplasm?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Tandem duplication resulting in a KIAA1549-BRAF gene fusion

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.label: E

explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO Grade 1) is the most common pediatric primary brain tumor, typically presenting in the cerebellum as a cystic mass with an enhancing mural nodule. The classic histological features are bipolar astrocytes with hair-like processes, eosinophilic corkscrew-shaped Rosenthal fibers, and granular bodies. The vast majority (>70%) harbor a KIAA1549-BRAF gene fusion that constitutively activates the MAPK/ERK pathway.
high_yield_pearl: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a benign pediatric cerebellar tumor (cystic with mural nodule, Rosenthal fibers, GFAP+) driven by KIAA1549-BRAF gene fusion.

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with severe gait ataxia, papilledema, and vomiting. Neuroimaging identifies a hyperdense, avidly enhancing midline cerebellar vermian mass obstructing the fourth ventricle. Resection reveals sheets of small, round, blue cells with hyperchromatic nuclei forming Homer Wright rosettes and expressing synaptophysin. Following operative resection, what critical diagnostic staging evaluation must be performed prior to craniospinal radiotherapy?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Contrast-enhanced total neuroaxis spine MRI and CSF cytologic analysis

options.label: B
options.text: Whole-body 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET scan to evaluate bone metastases

options.label: C
options.text: High-resolution computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis

options.label: D
options.text: Bone marrow aspiration and core biopsy from posterior iliac crests

options.label: E
options.text: Urinary catecholamine metabolite quantification for pheochromocytoma

explanation: Medulloblastoma is a WHO Grade 4 primitive embryonal neuroepithelial tumor (small round blue cells, Homer Wright rosettes, synaptophysin+) originating in the cerebellar vermis. It has a high propensity to disseminate through CSF pathways across the craniospinal axis ('drop metastases' to cauda equina). Full staging requires total neuroaxis spinal MRI and lumbar CSF cytology (obtained post-operatively once mass effect is relieved).
high_yield_pearl: Medulloblastoma (small round blue cells, Homer Wright rosettes) carries high risk for CSF seeding ('drop metastases'), requiring total neuroaxis MRI and CSF cytology.

stem: In the patient described with central pontine myelinolysis, neurological examination reveals intact alertness, flaccid quadriparesis, bilateral facial paralysis, complete loss of horizontal saccades, but intact vertical gaze and voluntary eyelid elevation. Which anatomical region's preservation allows maintenance of vertical eye movements and consciousness in this locked-in state?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Paramedian pontine reticular formation and bilateral abducens nuclei in the dorsal caudal pons

options.label: B
options.text: Rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF, oculomotor nuclei, and ascending reticular activating system in the midbrain

options.label: C
options.text: Inferior cerebellar peduncles and bilateral vestibular nuclei within the rostral medulla oblongata

options.label: D
options.text: Corticobulbar tracts traversing the middle cerebellar peduncles to the trigeminal motor nuclei

options.label: E
options.text: Descending tectospinal and vestibulospinal tracts traversing the anterior funiculus of the spinal cord

explanation: Central pontine myelinolysis destroys the basis pontis (corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts) and can involve horizontal gaze centers in the pontine tegmentum (PPRF and CN VI). However, vertical eye movements are mediated by the rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (riMLF) and the oculomotor/trochlear complexes in the midbrain tegmentum, which receive blood from the posterior cerebral artery and are anatomically rostral to the pontine lesion. The midbrain reticular activating system is also spared, preserving alertness (locked-in syndrome).
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 14-year-old girl is evaluated for progressive painless vision loss in her left eye. Physical examination demonstrates eight café-au-lait macules greater than 1.5 cm across her trunk, dense axillary freckling, and multiple raised dome-shaped brown iris hamartomas. Contrast-enhanced MRI reveals diffuse thickening and enhancement of the left optic nerve consistent with an optic pathway glioma. The protein normally encoded by the gene mutated in this condition acts primarily through which cellular mechanism?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Accelerating the hydrolysis of active Ras-GTP to inactive Ras-GDP

options.label: B
options.text: Phosphorylating p53 to initiate apoptotic arrest during DNA damage

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Forming an E3 ubiquitin ligase targeting hypoxia-inducible factors

options.label: E

explanation: This patient has Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1, von Recklinghausen disease) due to an autosomal dominant mutation in NF1 on chromosome 17q11. NF1 encodes neurofibromin, a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) that hydrolyzes active Ras-GTP to inactive Ras-GDP. Loss of neurofibromin leads to constitutive Ras activation and uncontrolled cell proliferation, manifesting as café-au-lait spots, axillary freckling (Crowe sign), Lisch nodules, and optic pathway gliomas.
high_yield_pearl: NF1 (chromosome 17) encodes neurofibromin, a Ras-GAP that inactivates Ras-GTP; loss leads to constitutive Ras hyperactivation, optic gliomas, and Lisch nodules.

stem: A 71-year-old right-handed man presents with acute difficulty communicating. His speech is non-fluent, slow, telegraphic, and effortful, but his auditory comprehension is intact and he follows complex multi-step commands. On physical examination, he has a dense right lower facial droop and right upper extremity hemiparesis (2/5 strength) with preserved lower extremity strength (5/5). What specific arterial branch has been occluded?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Superior division of the left middle cerebral artery

options.label: B
options.text: Inferior division of the left middle cerebral artery

options.label: C
options.text: Main trunk of the left anterior cerebral artery

options.label: D
options.text: Cortical branches of the left posterior cerebral artery

options.label: E
options.text: Perforating branches of the left anterior choroidal artery

explanation: The middle cerebral artery (MCA) bifurcates into superior and inferior divisions. The superior division supplies the frontal lobe convexity, including Broca area (pars opercularis/triangularis in the inferior frontal gyrus) and the motor cortex for the face and arm. Occlusion of the dominant superior MCA division produces expressive (Broca) non-fluent aphasia combined with contralateral face and arm weakness, while comprehension is preserved.
high_yield_pearl: Superior division MCA stroke causes Broca (expressive/non-fluent) aphasia with contralateral face and arm weakness, sparing comprehension.

stem: A 63-year-old man presents with acute right-sided hemiparesis sparing his face. Examination shows 0/5 strength in the right arm and leg with a right Babinski sign, loss of vibration and joint position sense on the right side of his body, and flaccid atrophy of the left side of his tongue, which deviates to the left upon protrusion. Pain and temperature sensation are preserved bilaterally. Which vessel is occluded in this classic medial medullary syndrome?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Paramedian branches of the anterior spinal artery in the anterior medulla

options.label: B
options.text: Circumferential branches of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery

options.label: C
options.text: Labyrinthine internal auditory branch of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery

options.label: D
options.text: Paramedian perforating branches of the rostral basilar artery trunk

options.label: E

explanation: Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome is caused by occlusion of the anterior spinal artery (ASA) or vertebral artery paramedian branches. The ischemic territory involves: 1) the medullary pyramid (contralateral hemiparesis of limbs, sparing face), 2) the medial lemniscus (contralateral loss of vibration and proprioception), and 3) the exiting hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) fibers/nucleus, causing ipsilateral tongue weakness with deviation toward the side of the lesion ('lick the lesion').
high_yield_pearl: Medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal artery stroke) presents with contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral proprioception loss, and ipsilateral tongue deviation.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with persistent pulsatile tinnitus described as a 'heartbeat in the ear', severe retro-orbital headache, and progressive redness and proptosis of her left eye. A loud vascular bruit is auscultated over her left mastoid and temporal bones. Catheter cerebral angiography confirms a direct pathological arteriovenous shunt between branches of the external carotid artery and the transverse-sigmoid dural sinus without an intervening capillary bed. What is the fundamental hemodynamic driver of her clinical symptoms?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: High-pressure arterial inflow causing retrograde hypertension within the dural venous system

options.label: B
options.text: Hypoperfusion of the inner ear cochlea from systemic arterial steal through the shunt

options.label: C
options.text: Severe intracranial hypotension from continuous cerebrospinal fluid leak into the sinus

options.label: D
options.text: Compression of the cochlear nerve by a cavernous internal carotid artery pseudoaneurysm

explanation: A dural arteriovenous fistula (dAVF) is an acquired vascular malformation where meningeal arteries (e.g., branches of external carotid) shunt high-pressure arterial blood directly into a dural venous sinus (most commonly the transverse, sigmoid, or cavernous sinus). Pulsatile tinnitus results from turbulent high-flow shunting near the temporal bone. Retrograde venous hypertension engorges cortical and orbital veins, carrying a high risk of intracranial hemorrhage and ophthalmic venous stasis.
high_yield_pearl: Dural arteriovenous fistulas shunt high-pressure arterial blood into dural sinuses, causing pulsatile tinnitus, retro-orbital pain, and retrograde venous hypertension.

stem: A 69-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset left-sided weakness. Physical examination reveals dense flaccid paralysis (0/5) and complete loss of pinprick and vibration sensation in her left lower extremity, but only mild clumsiness (4+/5) with normal sensation in her left face and upper extremity. She exhibits marked abulia and urinary incontinence. Occlusion of which cerebral artery accounts for this somatotopic pattern of motor and sensory loss?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.text: Right anterior cerebral artery supplying the medial paracentral lobule

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

explanation: The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the medial aspect of the primary motor and somatosensory cortices (the paracentral lobule). Because the motor and sensory homunculi represent the lower extremity and perineum along this medial surface, ACA infarction selectively causes contralateral lower extremity paralysis, sensory loss, and frontal urinary incontinence, sparing the face and arm (represented laterally along MCA territory).
high_yield_pearl: Anterior cerebral artery (ACA) stroke causes contralateral lower extremity motor and sensory loss, urinary incontinence, and abulia, sparing the face and arm.

stem: A 33-year-old woman presents with progressive left hemiparesis and mild headache over 2 weeks. Brain MRI reveals a solitary 4-cm subcortical white matter lesion with surrounding vasogenic edema. Contrast administration demonstrates an incomplete, open 'horseshoe-shaped' ring of enhancement whose open border faces the cerebral cortex. Stereotactic biopsy of the lesion is most likely to reveal which histopathologic finding?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

A key diagnostic radiologic sign is an 'open-ring' or 'horseshoe' enhancement, where the non-enhancing open arc points toward the cortical gray matter. Biopsy confirms demyelination: abundant myelin-clearing foamy macrophages (foamy histiocytes), reactive gliosis (Creutzfeldt-Peters cells), and critical relative preservation of underlying neurofilament axons (unlike GBM, which destroys both axons and myelin).

stem: A 16-year-old girl with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy managed with valproic acid presents with progressive stupor, vomiting, and flapping asterixis. Serum transaminases (AST and ALT), total bilirubin, and synthetic coagulation parameters are completely normal, but her serum ammonia level is markedly elevated at 195 umol/L. What enzyme in the urea cycle does valproic acid metabolite indirectly inhibit to cause this non-cirrhotic hyperammonemia?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.text: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I via depletion of N-acetylglutamate cofactor

options.label: B
options.text: Ornithine transcarbamylase via direct active-site competitive antagonism

options.label: C
options.text: Argininosuccinate synthetase via consumption of cytosolic ATP stores

high_yield_pearl: Valproate can cause non-cirrhotic hyperammonemic encephalopathy by depleting N-acetylglutamate, inhibiting carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the urea cycle.

stem: A 51-year-old woman presents with progressive right-sided sensorineural hearing loss, unsteadiness, mild facial asymmetry, and an absent right corneal reflex. MRI reveals a 3.5-cm well-circumscribed mass centered within the right cerebellopontine angle, expanding the internal acoustic meatus. Biopsy demonstrates alternating dense cellular zones with nuclear palisading (Verocay bodies) and hypocellular myxoid regions, staining strongly positive for S100 protein. From which embryologic precursor cells did this neoplasm originate?

Acoustic schwannomas typically arise from the vestibular division of CN VIII at the cerebellopontine angle.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with sudden left-sided weakness, dense left hemisensory loss to pinprick and proprioception, and a complete left homonymous hemianopia with macular involvement. Pupillary light reflexes are normal. Diffusion MRI demonstrates an ischemic stroke involving the posterior limb of the internal capsule, optic tract, and lateral geniculate nucleus. What specific vessel, arising directly from the internal carotid artery, has undergone occlusion?

options.label: B

Occlusion produces the classic anterior choroidal artery stroke triad: contralateral hemiparesis (corticospinal fibers), contralateral hemisensory loss (thalamocortical projections), and contralateral homonymous hemianopia (LGN/optic tract).

Which cerebellar region and afferent tract have undergone selective neurodegeneration?
