options.text: Anterior superior vermis and dorsal spinocerebellar afferents

options.label: B
options.text: Flocculonodular cortex and primary labyrinthine afferents

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral hemisphere cortex and corticopontine afferents

options.label: D
options.text: Posterior inferior vermis and olivocerebellar afferents

options.label: E
options.text: Dentate projection nucleus and rubrospinal afferents

explanation: Chronic alcohol neurotoxicity causes selective degeneration of Purkinje cells in the anterior and superior vermis (spinocerebellum), which receives lower extremity somatosensory inputs via dorsal spinocerebellar tracts. This selectively disrupts lower extremity coordination and gait while sparing the lateral cerebrocerebellar hemispheres that coordinate upper extremity fine motor movements and speech articulation.
high_yield_pearl: Alcoholic cerebellar degeneration selectively affects the anterior superior vermis, leading to truncal and lower limb gait ataxia with relative sparing of upper limb coordination and speech.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis presents with 4 days of painful right eye movements, central scotoma, and 4/5 left leg weakness. Visual acuity is 20/200 in the right eye, and swinging-flashlight testing reveals a right afferent pupillary defect. Intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone is initiated. What is the primary cellular mechanism by which this acute therapy accelerates neurological recovery?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Direct induction of rapid Schwann cell proliferation and axonal remyelination

options.label: B
options.text: Reduction of capillary endothelial permeability and suppression of inflammatory cytokines

options.label: C
options.text: Selective cytotoxicity and irreversible clonal deletion of memory B-lymphocytes

options.label: D
options.text: Competitive blockade of sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors on circulating leukocytes

options.label: E
options.text: Neutralization of circulating autoantibodies against aquaporin-4 water channels

explanation: High-dose intravenous corticosteroids (methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 3-5 days) treat acute MS relapses by rapidly stabilizing the blood-brain barrier (decreasing endothelial capillary permeability), downregulating pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma), and inhibiting T-cell activation and trafficking. Corticosteroids do not stimulate remyelination, delete B-cells (unlike anti-CD20 agents), or block S1P receptors (fingolimod mechanism).
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 28-year-old postpartum woman on oral contraceptives presents with worsening diffuse headache, bilateral papilledema, bilateral lower extremity weakness, and focal motor seizures. Contrast-enhanced CT venogram demonstrates non-filling of the posterior superior sagittal sinus surrounded by enhancing collateral dural channels ('empty delta sign'). What hemodynamic cascade causes parenchymal infarction and hemorrhage in cerebral venous sinus thrombosis?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Elevated retrograde venous capillary pressure causing vasogenic edema and hemorrhage

options.label: B
options.text: Primary arterial vasoconstriction mediated by excessive endothelin-1 secretion

options.label: C
options.text: Direct rupture of high-pressure Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms in basal ganglia

options.label: D
options.text: Obstruction of the foramen of Monro causing acute bilateral non-communicating hydrocephalus

options.label: E
options.text: Retrograde embolization of venous thrombi across a patent foramen ovale

explanation: Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis blocks the primary cerebral venous drainage pathway. Occlusion leads to severe retrograde venous and capillary hypertension, disruption of the blood-brain barrier (vasogenic edema), decreased cerebral perfusion pressure (cytotoxic edema), and eventually venous capillary rupture producing hemorrhagic venous infarction, typically in parasagittal convexities (bilateral leg weakness/seizures). Contrast CT shows the pathognomonic 'empty delta sign'.
high_yield_pearl: Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis ('empty delta sign') causes severe venous hypertension, cerebral edema, and bilateral parasagittal hemorrhagic venous infarcts.

stem: A 65-year-old man with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden visual loss on his left side. Visual field testing confirms a complete left homonymous hemianopia; however, formal perimetry demonstrates that central visual acuity across the central five degrees of the visual field remains completely intact at 20/20 (macular sparing). What physiological vascular collateral accounts for the preservation of central vision following this posterior cerebral artery infarct?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Dual blood supply to the occipital pole provided by terminal middle cerebral branches

options.label: B
options.text: Retrograde flow through anterior communicating artery to the calcarine cortex

options.label: C
options.text: Anastomotic supply from the superior cerebellar artery across tentorium cerebelli

options.label: D
options.text: Persistent embryologic trigeminal artery supplying the striate visual center

options.label: E
options.text: Reciprocal collateral branches from the anterior choroidal capillary plexus

explanation: The primary visual cortex along the calcarine sulcus is supplied by the calcarine branch of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). However, the representation of the macula at the occipital pole has dual vascular collateral supply from terminal branches of the middle cerebral artery (MCA). Thus, embolic occlusion of the PCA produces homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing because MCA collateral flow preserves the occipital pole.
high_yield_pearl: PCA calcarine stroke produces homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing due to collateral perfusion of the occipital pole by the middle cerebral artery.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive left hemiparesis and morning headaches over three weeks. Brain MRI shows a 5-cm irregularly rim-enhancing right frontal mass with extensive central necrosis and significant surrounding vasogenic edema. Biopsy shows dense GFAP immunoreactivity, microvascular proliferation forming glomeruloid vascular tufts, and hypercellular zones of tumor cells pseudopalisading around geographic areas of ischemic necrosis. What is the cell of origin of this malignancy?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Astrocyte undergoing dedifferentiation driven by oncogenic driver mutations

options.label: B
options.text: Oligodendrocyte with secondary loss of chromosome 1p and 19q arms

options.label: C
options.text: Arachnoid cap cell invading through the frontal meningeal dura mater

options.label: D
options.text: Microglial cell derived from primitive yolk sac myeloid progenitors

options.label: E
options.text: Pericyte proliferating within capillary basal lamina of the neocortex

explanation: Glioblastoma (Grade 4 astrocytoma) arises from astrocytes (or neural stem cell progenitors acquiring astrocytic differentiation), as demonstrated by intense immunohistochemical staining for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). The diagnostic hallmarks are pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular (endothelial) proliferation.
high_yield_pearl: Glioblastoma originates from astrocytes, stains positive for GFAP, and is characterized by pseudopalisading necrosis and glomeruloid microvascular proliferation.

stem: A 49-year-old man who experiences acute basilar artery thrombosis develops total quadriplegia, aphonia, and bilateral horizontal gaze paralysis. However, he is fully conscious, perfectly alert, and able to reliably communicate complex thoughts by blinking his upper eyelids and making voluntary vertical saccades. Why are consciousness and vertical ocular movements preserved despite extensive infarction of the ventral basis pontis ('locked-in' syndrome)?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Midbrain reticular activating system and rostral CN III/IV centers are spared

options.label: B
options.text: Horizontal saccade centers in the caudal pontine reticular formation are spared

options.label: C
options.text: Descending corticospinal tracts receive retrograde supply from anterior spinal artery

options.label: D
options.text: Medullary olive maintains tonic compensatory activation of cranial motor nuclei

options.label: E
options.text: Basal ganglia striosomes autonomously control cognitive processing and alertness

explanation: Locked-in syndrome results from bilateral ventral pontine infarction (basis pontis), transecting descending corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers, and destroying bilateral abducens nuclei/PPRF (loss of horizontal gaze). Patients cannot move limbs, speak, or look horizontally. However, consciousness (ascending reticular activating system in the dorsal midbrain) and vertical eye movements/eyelid opening (CN III/IV and rostral interstitial nucleus of MLF in the midbrain) are preserved because the midbrain receives rostral collateral perfusion from the posterior cerebral arteries.
high_yield_pearl: Locked-in syndrome spares consciousness (midbrain reticular activating system) and vertical eye movements (midbrain CN III/riMLF) despite bilateral pontine base destruction.

stem: A 36-year-old HIV-infected man with a CD4 count of 28/uL presents with progressive confusion and right-sided hemiparesis. Brain MRI reveals a solitary 3.8-cm periventricular rim-enhancing lesion with extensive surrounding edema. CSF testing is strongly positive for Epstein-Barr virus DNA by PCR. Empiric antitoxoplasmosis therapy produces no reduction in lesion volume after two weeks. Stereotactic biopsy is performed. Which histopathologic finding is most likely to be observed?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Dense angiocentric infiltrates of atypical B-lymphocytes expressing CD20

options.label: B
options.text: Encapsulated yeasts with mucopolysaccharide capsules clearing on mucicarmine

options.label: C
options.text: Intracellular pseudocysts containing crescents of Toxoplasma gondii bradyzoites

options.label: D
options.text: Extensive demyelination with oligodendrocytes containing glassy inclusions

options.label: E
options.text: Large syncytial cells with multiple eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions

explanation: Primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL) is an aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL, CD20+) strongly linked to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) in severely immunocompromised patients (HIV CD4 < 50/uL). PCNSL characteristically presents as a solitary periventricular ring-enhancing mass (unlike toxoplasmosis, which is typically multiple and responds to pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine). Detection of EBV DNA in CSF has high specificity for PCNSL.
high_yield_pearl: In HIV patients with CD4 < 50, a solitary periventricular ring-enhancing lesion with CSF EBV DNA is primary CNS lymphoma (CD20+ DLBCL).

stem: A 60-year-old man who suffered an ischemic lacunar stroke in his left posterolateral thalamus initially presented with contralateral hemianesthesia. Three months later, he presents with excruciating, burning, intractable pain over his right arm, trunk, and leg. Physical examination reveals that even the light touch of a cotton swab or a cool breeze elicits unbearable pain (allodynia and hyperpathia). What vascular perforator branches supplied the thalamic nucleus that underwent infarction?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Thalamogeniculate perforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery

options.label: B
options.text: Lenticulostriate branches of the proximal middle cerebral artery

options.label: C
options.text: Anterior communicating artery perforators supplying the optic chiasm

options.label: D
options.text: Paramedian basilar perforators supplying the dorsal pontine tegmentum

options.label: E
options.text: Anterior spinal artery branches supplying the medial medullary pyramid

explanation: Dejerine-Roussy syndrome (thalamic pain syndrome) occurs weeks to months after an ischemic stroke involving the ventral posterolateral (VPL) and ventral posteromedial (VPM) nuclei of the thalamus, which are supplied by the thalamogeniculate perforating branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). After initial contralateral sensory loss, central sensitization and loss of thalamic gating cause severe, paroxysmal, burning neuropathic pain and allodynia.
high_yield_pearl: Dejerine-Roussy syndrome (central post-stroke pain) occurs after thalamogeniculate PCA stroke damaging the VPL/VPM sensory thalamic nuclei.

stem: A 30-year-old man with refractory focal epilepsy receives an antiseizure medication that does not alter voltage-gated sodium channels or GABA receptor kinetics. Instead, it selectively binds to a specific integral transmembrane glycoprotein residing on presynaptic synaptic vesicles, inhibiting calcium-dependent neurotransmitter exocytosis. What is the molecular pharmacological target of this drug?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Synaptic vesicle protein 2A targeted by levetiracetam

options.label: B
options.text: Alpha-2-delta auxiliary calcium channel subunit targeted by gabapentin

options.label: C
options.text: GABA transporter 1 reuptake pump targeted by tiagabine

options.label: D
options.text: AMPA-type ionotropic glutamate receptor targeted by perampanel

options.label: E
options.text: Neuronal potassium channel subfamily KCNQ2/3 targeted by ezogabine

explanation: Levetiracetam (Keppra) has a unique mechanism of action: it binds stereoselectively to synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A) on presynaptic vesicles. This modulates synaptic vesicle fusion and reduces the calcium-dependent release of excitatory neurotransmitters (such as glutamate) during high-frequency epileptiform trains.
high_yield_pearl: Levetiracetam binds presynaptic vesicle protein SV2A, inhibiting glutamate exocytosis.

stem: A 29-year-old man started on carbamazepine for focal epilepsy achieves complete seizure cessation with a therapeutic serum level of 8 mcg/mL at two weeks. By week six, despite strict medication adherence confirmed by pill counts, his focal seizures recur and his trough level drops to 3.5 mcg/mL. What pharmacological mechanism accounts for this reduction in circulating drug concentration?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Auto-induction of hepatic CYP3A4 accelerating its own metabolic clearance

options.label: B
options.text: Saturation of intestinal carrier-mediated mucosal absorption receptors

options.label: C
options.text: Gradual induction of renal tubular clearance via proton-coupled antiport

options.label: D
options.text: Competitive displacement by endogenously synthesized steroid hormones

options.label: E
options.text: Tachyphylaxis from desensitization of central voltage-gated sodium channels

explanation: Carbamazepine is a potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, particularly CYP3A4, and crucially undergoes auto-induction (it induces the very enzymes responsible for its own metabolism). Auto-induction typically begins within 3-5 days and is complete by 3-5 weeks, shortening its elimination half-life from ~30 hours down to ~12-15 hours, necessitating dose adjustments.
high_yield_pearl: Carbamazepine induces its own hepatic metabolism (CYP3A4 auto-induction), causing serum levels to fall after 2-4 weeks and requiring upward titration.

stem: A 58-year-old man started on carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia three weeks ago presents with progressive lethargy, headache, and mild nausea. Serum electrolytes reveal a sodium of 122 mEq/L, serum osmolality of 252 mOsm/kg, and urine sodium of 46 mEq/L with urine osmolality of 520 mOsm/kg. He is euvolemic on examination. What mechanism accounts for this electrolyte abnormality?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis via enhanced renal collecting duct V2 response

options.label: B
options.text: Aldosterone receptor antagonism producing isolated mineralocorticoid resistance

options.label: C
options.text: Osmotic natriuresis secondary to competitive proximal tubule sodium cotransport

options.label: D
options.text: Drug-induced interstitial nephritis impairing medullary countercurrent gradients

options.label: E
options.text: Direct stimulation of central thirst osmoreceptors causing psychogenic polydipsia

explanation: Carbamazepine (and its derivative oxcarbazepine) is a well-known cause of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). Carbamazepine both increases hypothalamic release of vasopressin (ADH) and enhances the sensitivity of renal medullary collecting duct V2 receptors to circulating ADH, leading to excessive water reabsorption, concentrated urine (urine Osm >100), and euvolemic hypoosmolar hyponatremia.
high_yield_pearl: Carbamazepine can cause SIADH (euvolemic hyponatremia) by increasing ADH release and enhancing renal collecting duct V2 sensitivity.

stem: In an electrophysiologic study of cerebellar motor learning, microelectrodes in the Purkinje cell layer record all-or-none complex spikes featuring a high-amplitude primary action potential followed by small high-frequency wavelets. Which brainstem structure provides the monosynaptic excitatory climbing fiber inputs that generate these specific complex spikes?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Contralateral inferior olivary nucleus in the medullary tegmentum

options.label: B
options.text: Ipsilateral basal pontine nuclei within the ventral pontine bulge

options.label: C
options.text: Bilateral vestibular nuclear complex adjacent to fourth ventricle

options.label: D
options.text: Contralateral red nucleus within the rostral midbrain tegmentum

options.label: E
options.text: Ipsilateral dorsal motor vagal nucleus in the floor of fourth ventricle

explanation: Climbing fibers originate exclusively from the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla. Each Purkinje cell receives synaptic input from a single climbing fiber that wraps extensively around its dendritic tree, releasing aspartate/glutamate to evoke a powerful, prolonged all-or-none complex spike (error signal in motor learning).
high_yield_pearl: Climbing fibers originate exclusively from the contralateral inferior olivary nucleus and generate all-or-none complex spikes in Purkinje cells.

stem: In the induction management of cryptococcal meningoencephalitis, flucytosine is co-administered alongside amphotericin B to synergistically enhance fungal eradication. What is the precise molecular enzymatic pathway through which flucytosine exerts its selective cytotoxic action against fungal cells?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Conversion to 5-fluorouracil by fungal cytosine deaminase, inhibiting thymidylate synthase

options.label: B
options.text: Binding to membrane ergosterol to generate transmembrane ion-permeable channels

options.label: C
options.text: Inhibition of fungal 14-alpha-demethylase preventing conversion of lanosterol

options.label: D
options.text: Blockade of 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase disrupting the structural fungal cell wall

options.label: E
options.text: Disruption of mitotic spindle microtubules arresting fungal cells in metaphase

explanation: Flucytosine (5-fluorocytosine) enters fungal cells via cytosine permease and is converted into 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) by fungal cytosine deaminase (an enzyme absent in human cells). 5-FU is converted to 5-dUMP, which competitively inhibits thymidylate synthase, halting fungal DNA synthesis. Amphotericin B increases fungal cell membrane permeability, facilitating flucytosine entry.
high_yield_pearl: Flucytosine is converted by fungal cytosine deaminase to 5-FU, inhibiting thymidylate synthase and blocking fungal DNA synthesis.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is evaluated for acute spatial disorientation. She fails to acknowledge people standing on her left side, draws a clock face with all twelve numbers crowded into the right hemispace, and vehemently disowns her paralyzed left arm (anosognosia). Visual field examination reveals a left homonymous superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky'). What arterial division and neural pathway have been infarcted?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Inferior division of the right MCA damaging Meyer loop in the temporal lobe

options.label: B
options.text: Superior division of the right MCA damaging the frontoparietal operculum

options.label: C
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery damaging the dorsal supplementary motor cortex

options.label: D
options.text: Posterior cerebral artery damaging the dorsal optic radiations in parietal lobe

options.label: E
options.text: Anterior choroidal artery damaging the optic chiasm at the skull base

explanation: The non-dominant (typically right) MCA inferior division supplies the posterior temporal and inferior parietal lobes. Damage to the non-dominant parietal cortex produces severe contralateral spatial hemineglect and anosognosia. Concomitant injury to Meyer loop (the ventral optic radiation arching through the temporal lobe around the lateral ventricle) produces a contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky').
high_yield_pearl: Right inferior MCA division stroke produces left hemispatial neglect, anosognosia, and left superior quadrantanopia (Meyer loop damage).

stem: A 52-year-old man with untreated syphilis presents with shooting lancinating pains in his lower limbs, sensory ataxia, and a positive Romberg test. On pupillary examination, both pupils are small and irregular; they fail to constrict when exposed to bright flashlight beams but constrict promptly when focusing on a near object (Argyll Robertson pupils). Where is the neuropathological lesion localized that causes this light-near pupillary dissociation?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Pretectal nuclei of the dorsal midbrain interrupting the afferent light reflex

options.label: B
options.text: Edinger-Westphal nuclei within the ventral tegmentum of the upper midbrain

options.label: C
options.text: Ciliary ganglion within the posterior intraorbital fat adjacent to the optic nerve

options.label: D
options.text: Parasympathetic fibers traversing the superficial perimeter of cranial nerve III

options.label: E
options.text: Bilateral superior cervical sympathetic ganglia within the deep carotid sheath

explanation: Argyll Robertson pupils ('prostitute's pupils' — accommodate but do not react) are a classic hallmark of tabes dorsalis (tertiary neurosyphilis). The lesion localizes to the pretectal area of the dorsal midbrain, which relays light-reflex afferent signals from the optic tract to the bilateral Edinger-Westphal nuclei. Accommodation fibers enter more ventrally and are spared, preserving pupillary constriction to near targets.
high_yield_pearl: Argyll Robertson pupils in tabes dorsalis result from damage to the midbrain pretectal area, sparing ventral accommodation pathways (light-near dissociation).

stem: A 34-year-old man presents with acute confusion, bizarre behavior, fever, and olfactory hallucinations. Brain MRI shows asymmetric hyperintensity and petechial hemorrhage localized to the left anteromedial temporal and inferior frontal lobes. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with 450 RBCs/uL. He is immediately started on intravenous acyclovir. What viral enzyme is obligatorily required for the initial rate-limiting monophosphorylation of this therapeutic agent?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Herpesvirus thymidine kinase activating the acyclovir nucleoside analog

options.label: B
options.text: Host cell cellular kinase converting acyclovir directly into its active form

options.label: C
options.text: Viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase incorporating fraudulent purine bases

options.label: D
options.text: Host mitochondrial ribonucleotide reductase generating deoxyribonucleotides

options.label: E
options.text: Herpesvirus topoisomerase II unwinding double-stranded viral DNA strands

explanation: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) encephalitis causes hemorrhagic necrotizing encephalitis localized to the temporal and inferior frontal lobes. Treatment is immediate IV acyclovir. Acyclovir is a guanosine analogue that requires initial monophosphorylation by viral-encoded thymidine kinase. Host cellular kinases then convert it to acyclovir triphosphate, which selectively inhibits viral DNA polymerase and acts as a DNA chain terminator.
high_yield_pearl: HSV-1 temporal encephalitis is treated with acyclovir, which requires viral thymidine kinase for initial monophosphorylation before host kinases produce active triphosphate.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with persistent gait instability. On examination, when asked to stand with his feet together and eyes open, he immediately sways violently and requires examiner support to prevent falling. Closing his eyes does not significantly alter the severity of his severe postural swaying. Where is the lesion most likely localized?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Cerebellar midline vermis impairing central motor coordination

options.label: B
options.text: Cervical dorsal columns causing proprioceptive deafferentation

options.label: C
options.text: Bilateral peripheral large-fiber sensory polyneuropathy

options.label: D
options.text: Bilateral vestibular end-organs within membranous semicircular canals

options.label: E
options.text: Posterior root entry zones in the lumbar spinal cord

explanation: A true positive Romberg sign occurs when a patient is steady with eyes open but loses balance when eyes are closed, indicating sensory ataxia (dorsal column or peripheral proprioceptive loss). In cerebellar vermis lesions, patients exhibit cerebellar ataxia: they are unsteady with eyes open AND eyes closed because visual compensation cannot overcome central cerebellar motor incoordination.
high_yield_pearl: Cerebellar ataxia causes unsteadiness with eyes open and closed; sensory ataxia causes unsteadiness only after eyes are closed (positive Romberg).

stem: A 28-year-old woman develops a solitary demyelinating plaque selectively interrupting the left superior cerebellar peduncle. Neurophysiological testing demonstrates impaired unconscious proprioceptive feedback from Golgi tendon organs of the left lower extremity. By which pathway did this proprioceptive signal traverse the neuroaxis to reach this peduncle?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Ventral spinocerebellar tract crossing in cord and recrossing in peduncle

options.label: B
options.text: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract ascending uncrossed through the restiform body

options.label: C
options.text: Cuneocerebellar tract ascending uncrossed from lateral cuneate nucleus

options.label: D
options.text: Corticopontocerebellar pathway crossing within the ventral pontine tegmentum

options.label: E
options.text: Olivocerebellar pathway crossing within the medullary interolivary space

explanation: The ventral spinocerebellar tract transmits lower extremity Golgi tendon organ inputs (whole-limb motor feedback). It decussates in the anterior white commissure of the spinal cord, ascends to the rostral pons/midbrain, enters the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle, and decussates a second time to terminate in the ipsilateral cerebellar cortex (double cross).
high_yield_pearl: The ventral spinocerebellar tract double-crosses (first in spinal cord, second in superior cerebellar peduncle), conveying proprioceptive feedback to the ipsilateral cerebellum.

stem: A 64-year-old man is evaluated following an ischemic stroke. When given a printed book, he cannot read a single sentence or letter. However, when given a pen and paper, he writes a coherent, grammatically flawless paragraph describing his family; immediately thereafter, he is totally unable to read what he has just written. Which two neuroanatomical structures were infarcted to produce this classic disconnection syndrome (alexia without agraphia)?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Left primary visual cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum

options.label: B
options.text: Left angular gyrus and the arcuate fasciculus white matter tract

options.label: C
options.text: Left inferior temporal gyrus and the uncinate fasciculus fibers

options.label: D
options.text: Right visual cortex and the genu of the anterior corpus callosum

options.label: E
options.text: Bilateral superior temporal gyri and the transverse auditory radiation

explanation: Alexia without agraphia (pure word blindness) is a classic disconnection syndrome caused by a left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) infarction involving both the left primary visual cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum. The left visual field is processed by the intact right visual cortex, but visual information cannot cross to the left hemisphere language areas (angular gyrus) because the splenium is destroyed. Writing remains intact because the left angular gyrus and motor cortex are spared.
high_yield_pearl: Alexia without agraphia results from left PCA infarction damaging the left visual cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum.

stem: A 67-year-old woman with carotid atherosclerosis experiences sudden, painless loss of vision in her left eye, describing a 'dark shade or curtain descending from above' that leaves her completely blind for five minutes before spontaneously lifting. Immediate funduscopic examination reveals a bright, glistening, yellowish refractive crystal lodged at a bifurcation of a retinal arteriole (Hollenhorst plaque). Which arterial branch gave rise to the central retinal artery carrying this microembolus?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Ophthalmic artery arising as the first intradural branch of internal carotid artery

options.label: B
options.text: Superficial temporal artery arising from the bifurcation of external carotid artery

options.label: C
options.text: Middle meningeal artery entering the skull base through the foramen spinosum

options.label: D
options.text: Anterior cerebral artery arising from the internal carotid terminal bifurcation

options.label: E
options.text: Internal maxillary artery passing through the pterygopalatine fossa

explanation: Amaurosis fugax (transient monocular vision loss) is a classic manifestation of internal carotid artery (ICA) stenosis. Microemboli (cholesterol plaques/Hollenhorst plaques or platelet-fibrin thrombi) dislodge from the carotid bifurcation and travel through the ICA into its first major intradural branch, the ophthalmic artery, and lodge in the central retinal artery or its branches, causing transient retinal ischemia.
high_yield_pearl: Amaurosis fugax is transient monocular visual loss caused by microemboli (Hollenhorst plaques) traveling via the internal carotid artery to the ophthalmic and central retinal arteries.

stem: A 36-year-old woman experiences 3 weeks of intractable nausea, projectile vomiting, and continuous hiccups that fail to respond to antiemetic and prokinetic medications. Thorough gastroenterological evaluation is negative. Two weeks later, she develops bilateral optic neuritis. Which neuroanatomical region lacks an intact blood-brain barrier, permitting circulating anti-AQP4 antibodies to initiate her initial presentation?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Nucleus ambiguus located in the rostral ventrolateral medulla

options.label: B
options.text: Area postrema situated in the caudal floor of the fourth ventricle

options.label: C
options.text: Nucleus tractus solitarius receiving visceral sensory vagal afferents

options.label: D
options.text: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus nerve mediating parasympathetic tone

options.label: E
options.text: Inferior salivatory nucleus situated in the pontomedullary junction

explanation: The patient exhibits area postrema syndrome, a classic initial manifestation of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD). The area postrema is a circumventricular organ located in the caudal floor of the fourth ventricle. Because it lacks a blood-brain barrier and has fenestrated capillaries, it serves as the emetic chemoreceptor trigger zone and is uniquely exposed to circulating anti-AQP4 IgG antibodies, leading to astrocytopathy, intractable nausea, vomiting, and hiccups.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with progressive morning headaches, vomiting, and secondary torticollis. Brain MRI reveals an expansile mass arising from the floor of the fourth ventricle that extends out into the cerebellomedullary cistern through the foramina of Luschka. Biopsy demonstrates tumor cells arrayed in perivascular pseudorosettes with intracytoplasmic blepharoplasts (basal ciliary bodies). What is the primary route of metastatic dissemination characteristic of this neoplasm?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 3

options.label: A
options.text: Cerebrospinal fluid seeding along the craniospinal leptomeningeal subarachnoid space

options.label: B
options.text: Hematogenous spread via the retroperitoneal Batson vertebral venous plexus

options.label: C
options.text: Lymphatic drainage into the deep superior internal jugular cervical lymph nodes

options.label: D
options.text: Transdural invasion across the tentorium into the posterior sagittal sinus

options.label: E
options.text: Direct retrobulbar extension along the perineural sheaths of the optic nerve

explanation: Ependymomas arise from ependymal cells lining the ventricular system, most commonly the fourth ventricle in children. Histology features perivascular pseudorosettes (tumor cells arranged around blood vessels with fibrillary cuffs) and blepharoplasts. Because of their intraventricular location, they frequently disseminate throughout the subarachnoid space via CSF seeding along the spinal cord.
high_yield_pearl: Ependymomas arise in the 4th ventricle in children, show perivascular pseudorosettes and blepharoplasts, and disseminate via CSF pathways.

stem: A 35-year-old HIV-infected man with a baseline CD4 count of 18/uL completes two weeks of induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis, achieving sterile CSF cultures. Combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) is initiated. Three weeks later, his CD4 count rebounds to 190/uL, but he develops high fever, worsening headache, and intense new leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI, while repeat CSF cultures remain sterile. What is the immunological mechanism of this clinical deterioration?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Hyperinflammatory immune reaction against residual dead fungal antigens

options.label: B
options.text: Rapid emergence of flucytosine-resistant cryptococcal mutant strains

options.label: C
options.text: Direct neurotoxicity and chemical arachnoiditis induced by non-nucleosides

options.label: D
options.text: Development of acute cytomegalovirus ependymitis following viral reactivation

options.label: E
options.text: Secondary primary central nervous system lymphoma transformation

explanation: This patient has Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS). After starting ART in patients with profound immunodeficiency, rapid restoration of CD4+ T-cell counts and functional pathogen-specific cellular immunity triggers a paradoxical, hyperinflammatory cytokine storm against persistent non-viable antigen remnants of prior opportunistic infections (e.g., Cryptococcus, Mycobacteria). Treatment involves corticosteroids while continuing antimicrobial and antiretroviral therapy.
high_yield_pearl: IRIS occurs after ART initiation as recovering CD4+ T cells trigger a paradoxical hyperinflammatory reaction against residual dead microbial antigens.

stem: A 52-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder and malnutrition is admitted with stupor and a serum sodium of 104 mEq/L. Over the next 20 hours, intravenous hypertonic saline administration raises his serum sodium to 130 mEq/L. Three days later, he becomes mute, quadriplegic, and dysphagic, communicating only through vertical eye movements. What cellular biophysical mechanism directly initiates the demyelination in the basis pontis?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Intracellular brain edema resulting from rapid water influx into hypertonic astrocyte cell bodies

options.label: B
options.text: Acute cell shrinkage and oligodendrocyte apoptosis caused by rapid extracellular hyperosmotic fluid shift

options.label: C
options.text: Selective thrombotic occlusion of paramedian penetrating branches of the basilar artery

options.label: D
options.text: Excitotoxic excessive glutamate stimulation triggering neuronal calcium overload in pontine nuclei

options.label: E
options.text: Immune complex deposition inducing classical complement cascade activation along myelin sheaths

explanation: In chronic hyponatremia (>48 hours), brain cells adapt by extruding organic osmolytes (glutamate, myoinositol, taurine) to prevent cerebral edema. When serum sodium is corrected too rapidly (>8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours), the extracellular fluid becomes hyperosmolar relative to brain cells. Water shifts rapidly out of cells, causing severe dehydration and apoptosis of oligodendrocytes. The basis pontis is exquisitely vulnerable because intersecting transverse pontocerebellar and longitudinal corticospinal fibers create a rigid anatomic meshwork with little room for shrinkage without mechanical shear.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 32-year-old HIV-infected man with a CD4 count of 22/uL presents with delirium, confusion, lower extremity weakness, and urinary incontinence. Brain MRI shows thin periventricular subependymal enhancement lining the lateral and fourth ventricles. Histopathological examination of ventricular subependymal tissue demonstrates cytomegaly with prominent intranuclear basophilic inclusions surrounded by a clear halo ('owl-eye' appearance). What is the first-line therapeutic agent and its primary mechanism of action?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 4

options.label: A
options.text: Ganciclovir via inhibition of cytomegalovirus DNA polymerase chain elongation

options.label: B
options.text: Foscarnet via selective antagonism of viral pyrophosphate binding domains

options.label: C
options.text: Cidofovir via direct phosphorylation-independent incorporation into viral RNA

options.label: D
options.text: Acyclovir via selective activation by cytomegaloviral thymidine kinase

options.label: E
options.text: Ribavirin via competitive inhibition of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase

explanation: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) encephalitis / ventriculoependymitis occurs in advanced AIDS (CD4 < 50/uL), presenting with periventricular rim enhancement, confusion, and radiculopathy. Histology characteristically shows cytomegalic cells with prominent intranuclear basophilic inclusion bodies with halos ('owl-eye'). First-line therapy is intravenous ganciclovir, which is phosphorylated by viral UL97 kinase and inhibits viral DNA polymerase.
high_yield_pearl: CMV ventriculoencephalitis in advanced AIDS (CD4 < 50) presents with periventricular enhancement, 'owl-eye' inclusions, and is treated with ganciclovir.

stem: A 66-year-old man presents with sudden double vision and right-sided hemiplegia. On examination, his left eye is resting in a 'down-and-out' position with complete ptosis and a dilated, unreactive pupil (complete left third nerve palsy). His right arm and leg demonstrate flaccid paralysis (0/5 strength) with hyperreflexia and an extensor plantar response. Which arterial branch and midbrain structures were damaged to produce this Weber syndrome?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Paramedian PCA branches injuring the crus cerebri and fascicles of CN III

options.label: B
options.text: Quadrigeminal artery branches injuring the inferior colliculus and CN IV

options.label: C
options.text: Short circumferential basilar branches injuring the medial lemniscus and CN VI

options.label: D
options.text: Anterior choroidal artery branches injuring the optic tract and CN II

options.label: E
options.text: Superior cerebellar artery branches injuring the red nucleus and CN V

explanation: Weber syndrome (superior alternating hemiplegia) is a ventral midbrain syndrome caused by occlusion of paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) or basilar bifurcation. The infarct damages the cerebral peduncle / crus cerebri (corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, causing contralateral hemiplegia and contralateral lower facial droop) and exiting fascicles of the oculomotor nerve (CN III, causing ipsilateral 'down-and-out' pupil-dilated third nerve palsy).
high_yield_pearl: Weber syndrome is caused by a ventral midbrain PCA stroke, presenting with ipsilateral CN III palsy and contralateral hemiplegia.

stem: A 7-year-old girl has multiple daily episodes of blank staring lasting six seconds, accompanied by subtle rhythmic eye blinking, with immediate resumption of normal conversation and no postictal confusion. EEG shows generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges reliably provoked by hyperventilation. What is the precise molecular target of the first-line pharmacotherapeutic agent indicated for this condition?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Low-threshold T-type voltage-gated calcium channels in thalamic relay neurons

options.label: B
options.text: Presynaptic high-voltage-activated N-type calcium channels in the cortex

options.label: C
options.text: Postsynaptic GABA-A receptor chloride channels in the reticular nucleus

options.label: D
options.text: Fast-inactivating voltage-gated sodium channels in hippocampal CA1 neurons

options.label: E
options.text: Synaptic vesicle glycoprotein SV2A preventing vesicular glutamate release

explanation: This child has classic absence (petit mal) seizures characterized by brief staring spells without postictal confusion and 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG pattern. The first-line drug is ethosuximide. Ethosuximide specifically blocks low-threshold T-type voltage-gated calcium channels in thalamic relay neurons, disrupting the rhythmic thalamocortical oscillatory burst-firing that drives absence seizures.
high_yield_pearl: Ethosuximide is first-line for absence seizures and works by blocking low-threshold T-type calcium channels in thalamic relay neurons.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis presents with a sudden electric-shock-like sensation that shoots down her neck and spine into her legs whenever she bends her head forward to tie her shoes (Lhermitte sign). This symptom localizes to a demyelinating plaque in which spinal cord pathway?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Anterior corticospinal tract mediating axial motor tone and postural stability

options.label: B
options.text: Cervical dorsal columns producing mechanosensitive ectopic action potential discharge

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral spinothalamic tract conducting pain and temperature sensation from the trunk

options.label: D
options.text: Ventral spinocerebellar tract conveying unconscious proprioception from the limbs

options.label: E
options.text: Intermediolateral cell column supplying preganglionic sympathetic outflow to viscera

explanation: Lhermitte sign (a paroxysmal electric shock sensation triggered by neck flexion radiating down the spine and extremities) is a classic finding in multiple sclerosis. It indicates demyelination within the cervical spinal cord posterior columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus). Neck flexion exerts mechanical traction on demyelinated, hyperexcitable primary sensory axons lacking their normal insulating myelin sheath, triggering ectopic mechanosensitive action potential discharge.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 68-year-old man undergoes surgical repair of an extensive descending thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm. Post-operatively, he awakens with flaccid paraplegia (0/5 strength in both lower extremities), loss of pinprick and temperature sensation below the T10 dermatome, and acute urinary retention. However, his vibration and joint position sense remain completely intact bilaterally. Compromise of which radicular artery during aortic cross-clamping produced this anterior spinal artery syndrome?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 6

options.label: A
options.text: Great anterior radiculomedullary artery of Adamkiewicz originating from lower intercostals

options.label: B
options.text: Posterior spinal arteries arising directly from the posterior inferior cerebellar arteries

options.label: C
options.text: Vertebral artery ascending branches entering the transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae

options.label: D
options.text: Internal iliac lateral sacral branches supplying the pelvic cauda equina nerve roots

options.label: E
options.text: Ascending cervical radicular branches emerging from the thyrocervical trunk

explanation: The anterior spinal artery (ASA) supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord (anterior horns, corticospinal tracts, and spinothalamic tracts). In the lower thoracic and lumbar cord, the ASA relies heavily on the artery of Adamkiewicz (great anterior radiculomedullary artery), which typically arises from a left intercostal or lumbar artery between T9 and T12. Loss of this artery during thoracoabdominal aortic surgery causes anterior cord syndrome: paraplegia, loss of pain/temperature, and autonomic dysfunction, with complete sparing of the posterior dorsal columns.
high_yield_pearl: Anterior spinal artery syndrome during aortic surgery results from ischemia to the artery of Adamkiewicz, causing bilateral paraplegia and thermoanalgesia with preserved dorsal columns.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis is initiated on fingolimod. Baseline electrocardiography is obtained prior to the first dose because of transient bradycardia risks. What is the cellular pharmacological mechanism by which fingolimod reduces clinical relapse rates in multiple sclerosis?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Inhibition of dihydroorotate dehydrogenase arresting activated lymphocyte proliferation in S-phase

options.label: B
options.text: Internalization and degradation of sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors sequestering lymphocytes in lymph nodes

options.label: C
options.text: Selective antibody-dependent cytotoxicity against CD20-expressing mature circulating B-cells

options.label: D
options.text: Blockade of leukocyte alpha-4 integrins preventing vascular endothelial cell adhesion and migration

options.label: E
options.text: Alkylating DNA guanine residues to cross-link strands and trigger mature T-cell apoptosis

explanation: Fingolimod is an oral sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulator. It is phosphorylated in vivo and binds to S1P receptors (S1PR1, 3, 4, 5) on lymphocytes, causing receptor internalization and degradation. Without functional surface S1P1 receptors, lymphocytes cannot sense the S1P gradient between lymph nodes (low S1P) and plasma (high S1P) and are trapped within secondary lymphoid organs, preventing auto-reactive T and B cells from circulating into the central nervous system.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 62-year-old woman develops subacute, rapidly progressive truncal and limb ataxia, vertigo, and scanning dysarthria over four weeks. Brain MRI reveals no focal mass or stroke, but cerebrospinal fluid shows mild lymphocytic pleocytosis. Serum testing is strongly positive for anti-Yo antibodies (anti-Purkinje cell cytoplasmic antibodies). Which neoplasm is most likely occult in this patient?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Ovarian adenocarcinoma or high-grade serous carcinoma

options.label: B
options.text: Small cell lung carcinoma expressing neuroendocrine antigens

options.label: C
options.text: Thymoma associated with acetylcholine receptor autoantibodies

options.label: D
options.text: Hodgkin lymphoma expressing Reed-Sternberg cytoplasmic markers

options.label: E
options.text: Renal clear cell carcinoma with paraneoplastic erythrocytosis

explanation: Anti-Yo (PCA-1) antibodies target Purkinje cell cytoplasmic antigens CDR2 and CDR2L and are strongly associated with paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration in women with gynecologic malignancies (ovarian, fallopian, uterine) or breast carcinoma. Anti-Hu is associated with small cell lung cancer; anti-Tr is associated with Hodgkin lymphoma.
high_yield_pearl: Anti-Yo paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration causes rapid Purkinje cell loss and is most commonly associated with ovarian and breast carcinomas.

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with progressive cerebellar ataxia, choreoathetosis, recurrent severe sinopulmonary bacterial infections, and prominent conjunctival telangiectasias. Laboratory evaluation reveals marked deficiency of serum IgA and significantly elevated alpha-fetoprotein. What molecular cellular defect is responsible for this patient's disease?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Defective ATM kinase signaling in double-strand DNA break repair

options.label: B
options.text: Impaired nucleotide excision repair of ultraviolet DNA photoproducts

options.label: C
options.text: Trinucleotide GAA expansion impairing mitochondrial iron-sulfur biogenesis

options.label: D
options.text: Peroxisomal ATP-binding cassette transporter assembly failure

options.label: E
options.text: Lysosomal sphingomyelinase deficiency causing lipid storage in neurons

explanation: Ataxia-telangiectasia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATM gene on chromosome 11q22. ATM encodes a serine/threonine protein kinase involved in sensing double-stranded DNA breaks and initiating cell-cycle checkpoint arrest/repair. Defective repair causes cerebellar Purkinje cell loss, immunodeficiency (low IgA), telangiectasias, elevated AFP, and sensitivity to ionizing radiation.
high_yield_pearl: Ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM mutation) impairs double-strand DNA break repair, causing cerebellar ataxia, telangiectasias, recurrent infections, low IgA, and high AFP.

stem: A 59-year-old man presents with sudden acute vertigo, nausea, hoarseness, left facial numbness, and severe left-sided limb ataxia. Physical examination reveals left-sided Horner syndrome, left vocal cord paralysis, and decreased pinprick sensation over the right arm and leg. What specific cerebellar input structure damaged in the dorsolateral medulla explains his left limb ataxia?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 2

options.label: A
options.text: Inferior cerebellar peduncle within the dorsolateral medullary rim

options.label: B
options.text: Middle cerebellar peduncle transversing the ventral pons

options.label: C
options.text: Superior cerebellar peduncle descending from midbrain tegmentum

options.label: D
options.text: Medial longitudinal fasciculus adjacent to the median raphe

options.label: E
options.text: Ventral tegmental decussation of rubrospinal motor fibers

explanation: This patient has lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome due to occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery. The ipsilateral limb ataxia is caused by infarction of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (restiform body), which carries spinocerebellar and olivocerebellar inputs into the cerebellum.
high_yield_pearl: In Wallenberg syndrome (PICA infarct), ipsilateral limb ataxia is caused by damage to the inferior cerebellar peduncle (restiform body).

stem: A 62-year-old man experiences a two-minute focal motor seizure involving clonic contractions of his left face and left upper extremity. Immediately following seizure cessation, he has a flaccid left hemiplegia and left facial droop with normal consciousness. Non-contrast head CT and CT angiography show no acute intracranial hemorrhage or large vessel occlusion. Over the subsequent four hours, his motor strength recovers completely to 5/5. What is the physiological mechanism of this transient postictal paresis (Todd paralysis)?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Transient motor cortex neuronal metabolic exhaustion and active synaptic hyperpolarization

options.label: B
options.text: Spontaneous thromboembolic occlusion followed by rapid endogenous tissue tPA lysis

options.label: C
options.text: Transient compression of the corticospinal tract by acute focal vasogenic edema

options.label: D
options.text: Acute depletion of acetylcholine stores at the skeletal neuromuscular junction

options.label: E
options.text: Reversible demyelinating conduction block along the descending internal capsule

explanation: Todd paralysis (Todd paresis) is a transient focal neurological deficit (most commonly motor weakness) following a seizure, typically lasting minutes to a few hours (rarely up to 24-48 hours). The pathophysiology involves prolonged postictal neuronal depression, energy/metabolite (ATP, glucose) exhaustion in overactivated epileptogenic motor networks, and intense, active GABAergic synaptic hyperpolarization.
high_yield_pearl: Todd paralysis is transient postictal focal paresis caused by localized neuronal metabolic exhaustion and synaptic hyperpolarization following a seizure.

stem: A 41-year-old woman presents with bilateral sequential visual loss and severe paraparesis. Spinal MRI demonstrates a continuous T2 hyperintensity extending from C2 to T1, and serum testing reveals high-titer autoantibodies against aquaporin-4 (AQP4). Which disease-modifying therapy commonly prescribed for multiple sclerosis is contraindicated because it can precipitate catastrophic, fulminant relapses in this condition?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Eculizumab targeting the terminal complement protein C5

options.label: B
options.text: Rituximab directed against the CD20 surface antigen on B-lymphocytes

options.label: C
options.text: Fingolimod sequestering lymphocytes within secondary lymphoid organs

options.label: D
options.text: Mycophenolate mofetil inhibiting inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase

options.label: E
options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone administered during acute exacerbations

explanation: The patient has neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), characterized by anti-AQP4 autoantibodies and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM >=3 vertebral segments). Standard MS therapies such as fingolimod, natalizumab, and interferon-beta can paradoxically trigger severe, life-threatening exacerbations in NMOSD by augmenting humoral and astrocytic inflammation. NMOSD maintenance therapy relies on B-cell depletion (rituximab), IL-6 receptor blockade (satralizumab), complement C5 inhibition (eculizumab), or immunosuppressants (mycophenolate mofetil).
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 31-year-old woman with a history of optic neuritis 2 years ago reports that whenever she takes a hot bath or exercises vigorously, her vision in the right eye becomes markedly blurry and washed-out. After resting in an air-conditioned room for 30 minutes, her vision returns completely to baseline. Which biophysical principle explains this transient phenomenon?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 1

options.label: A
options.text: Thermal vasodilation shunting blood away from the ophthalmic artery causing retinal ischemia

options.label: B
options.text: Temperature elevation accelerates sodium channel inactivation, reducing the action potential safety factor in demyelinated axons

options.label: C
options.text: Heat-induced breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier permitting acute complement infiltration

options.label: D
options.text: Hyperthermia stimulates aberrant cross-talk and ephaptic transmission between adjacent motor nerves

options.label: E
options.text: Thermal denaturation of myelin basic protein causing temporary structural dissolution of lamellae

explanation: This patient is demonstrating Uhthoff phenomenon, where heat or physical exertion transiently worsens pre-existing demyelinating deficits. Along demyelinated nerve segments, voltage-gated sodium channels are dispersed, lowering the safety factor for action potential propagation. Modest temperature elevations (even 0.5 degrees C) accelerate the kinetics of sodium channel inactivation and shorten action potential duration, causing conduction block across demyelinated optic nerve segments that reverses upon cooling.
high_yield_pearl: High-Yield Rule: Unit 01: Demyelinating Diseases

stem: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department in continuous generalized convulsive status epilepticus lasting twelve minutes. Two successive intravenous doses of lorazepam temporarily halt her motor convulsions, but continuous generalized rhythmic jerking resumes eight minutes later. What is the most appropriate next step in the established pharmacotherapeutic algorithm?
source: Neuro E3 Higher-Order Master Bank Unit 5

options.label: A
options.text: Administer an intravenous loading infusion of fosphenytoin or levetiracetam

options.label: B
options.text: Administer repeated doses of intravenous diazepam every fifteen minutes

options.label: C
options.text: Initiate emergent therapeutic hypothermia to suppress cerebral metabolism

options.label: D
options.text: Perform emergent endotracheal intubation with oral carbamazepine loading

options.label: E
options.text: Inject intramuscular flumazenil to reverse allosteric receptor saturation

explanation: In established status epilepticus, first-line therapy is an intravenous benzodiazepine (lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg or diazepam). If seizures continue or recur beyond 5-10 minutes, second-line therapy is an urgent non-sedating intravenous antiseizure medication, specifically fosphenytoin (20 mg PE/kg), levetiracetam (60 mg/kg), or valproate (40 mg/kg). Benzodiazepines should not be endlessly repeated because GABA-A receptors undergo rapid internalization during prolonged seizures.
high_yield_pearl: Status epilepticus failing initial benzodiazepines requires emergent second-line loading with IV fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, or valproate.
